laws.title: St. John’s-St. Luke Evangelical Church Historic District
laws.content:
(a) An historic district to be known as the St. John’s-St. Luke Evangelical Church Historic District is hereby established in accordance with the provisions of this article.

(b) This historic district designation is hereby certified as being consistent with the Detroit Master Plan of Policies.

(c) The boundaries of the St. John’s-St. Luke Evangelical Church Historic District, as shown on the map on file in the Office of the City Clerk, are as follows:

On the southwest, the center line of Russell; on the northwest and west, the center line of Service; on the north, the northerly boundary of Lot 13 (extended west) of Fraser’s subdivision of part of the Guoin Farm; on the northeast, the northeast boundary of Lot 22 (extended southeast) of Fraser’s subdivision of part of the Guoin Farm; and on the southeast, the center line of the vacated Chestnut Street. (These boundaries include Lots 13, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27 of Fraser’s Subdivision of part of the Guoin Farm (L1/P30).

(d) The elements of design, as defined in Section 21-2-2 of this Code, shall be as follows:

(1) *Height.* The church is a single tall story; its tallest point is the southwest tower, approximately 55 feet tall. The attached school is three stories tall with additional height in the mansard roof. The parish house is $2\frac{1}{2}$ stories tall.

(2) *Proportion of building’s front façades.* The Russell façade of the church is taller than wide, the height being emphasized by the vertically proportioned nave and towers. On the southeast elevation along the parking lot and the northwest elevation along Service Street, the church is longer than tall, although the horizontal is visually equalized by the verticality of the transept arms and corner towers. The southeast elevation of the attached school is taller than wide, the vertical being emphasized by the two gables. The northeast elevation of the school is approximately two times wider than tall, excepting the roof. The front façade of the parish house is taller than wide to its front gable.

(3) *Proportion of openings within the façades.* No significant openings in the church, school and front façade of the parish house are wider than tall. Openings in the church are most often subdivided by tracery, louvers, or with more than one emphatically vertical element combined. The area of the openings in the Russell Street façade of the church comprise approximately 15 percent of the surface; the northeast elevation of the school is comprised of not more than 25 percent openings; the original two-over-two double hung wood sash windows are present. Approximately 30 percent of the front façade of the parish house is made up of openings.

(4) *Rhythm of solids to voids in front façades.* In the Russell Street façade of the church, the rhythm of voids in the solid is created by the formal arrangement of windows and entrances. A large tracery window is centered in the front façade above the projecting front entrance porch. A pointed arched transom set with stained glass in elaborate tracery rests above the entrance door. In the second stage of the tower on the south side of the façade is a pair of lancet windows situated above the double-pointed arch entrance in the first stage of the tower; a blind spherical triangular opening is centered in the third stage; and a louvered tracery window shields the bell chamber in the fourth stage. Pointed arch windows of the side aisles on the southeast elevation of the church are in pairs of two per bay; the four bays of the clerestory contain a coupled window with a Tudor arch each. In the transept arms are two lancet windows below a large squat ogee arch in elaborate tracery. In the connector between the church and the school is a staircase reflected on the exterior by the irregular and ascending windows of the first and second stories. The third story contains four regularly spaced lancet windows, the two center ones being of shorter height. Windows on the

CD21:79
§ 21-2-127

DETROIT CITY CODE

southeast and northwest elevation of the school are formally arranged in groups of three within the two bays, with one triangular window in each of the two frontal gables. The northeast elevation of the school has double-hung sash windows arranged regularly, one above the other. The southern portion of the front façade of the parsonage is brought forward with a recessed entrance porch on the north side and a single window on the south. A triple window is centered at the second-floor level. The gable above contains a small window with a Tudor arch. The recessed chamfered wing on the north has one window placed directly above the other on each face.

(5) Rhythm of spacing of buildings on streets. Inapplicable due to single-complex district.

(6) Rhythm of entrance and/or porch projections. Inapplicable due to single-complex district.

(7) Relationship of materials. The northwest and southeast elevations of the church are covered in formstone, an ashlar patterned, rock-faced concrete covering; the original brick surface has become exposed in some areas. The Russell Street façade is covered with perma-stone. The original slate roof is now covered with asphalt; original iron coping remains. Finials at gable peaks are metal. Sills, string courses, and corbels along the gables are sandstone. Window trim, elaborate tracery, and doors are wood. The two towers have copper roofs. Foundations of the school and church are limestone; the attached school building is brick with wood trim, has the original galvanized iron cornice, and has a tooled sandstone water table. Its roof is asphalt and there is an integral gutter system. The parish house is brick with wooden trim and a slate roof.

(8) Relationship of textures. The church contrasts rock-faced formstone and perma-stone and in some places exposed scored brick with the smoother surfaces of sandstone trim, dressed sandstone water tables, wooden window trim and tracery, and a smooth asphalt roof. Copper roofing on the towers also provides textural contrast. Contrast to the brick surface of the school is provided by the rock-faced ashlar foundations, dressed sandstone water table course and sills, wooden window frames, and raised brick corbelling. Textural interest is added to the painted brick surface of the parish house by the raised stone belt courses and raised brick window enframement, as well as the wooden trim.

(9) Relationship of colors. The gray-beige of the formstone and perma-stone surface of the church contrasts with the black roof and is highlighted by the green copper roofs of the towers. Wooden window trim is either gray or beige; tracery is a beige putty color. Orange brick is exposed by deteriorating formstone in various places. Some of the gray sandstone has blackened with age. Doors are generally painted in brown wood tones. The door in the connector between the church and school is painted gray. The aged reddish-orange brick of the school contrasts with the gray stone foundations, gray window trim, gray coping, and black roof. Traces of paint exist on the brick and stone. The parish house is painted gray; the ornamental and window trim is gray, the wooden steps are gray, and the foundations are gray stone.

(10) Relationship of architectural details. Details of the church and school are architectonic in character and in keeping with the Gothic style. Decorative corbelling trims the gables, voussoirs accentuate openings and sills, belt courses are pronounced, and finials crown the peaks of gables. Window treatment is one of the most ornamental features of the church and school; elaborate tracery exists in the church windows, wooden clerestory frames are treated decoratively, and the arrangements of lights in the southeast and northwest elevations of the school is decorative. The decorative brick corbelling of the school mimics the corbelling of the church and contrasts with the more utilitarian northeast elevation of the school, which displays corner pilasters and pilasters setting off the entrance bay. The parish house is austere in ornament; a molded brick frame extends around the second-story triple window, a string course extends around the building, and a gable window bears a Tudor arch. The recessed wing has a chamfered corner with brackets at the roofline.

(11) Relationship of roof shapes. The church has a steeply pitched gable roof with transept arms towards the altar end and roofed side aisles resulting in a clerestory above. A connecting addition with a hip roof joins the church and

CD21:80

laws.title: History
laws.content:
§ 21-2-127

school. The roof of the school is a mansard. Roofs on the parish house result in complex relationships; a pitched roof with a frontal gable is intersected by a hipped roof with a transverse gable.

(12) Walls of continuity. Inapplicable due to single-complex district.

(13) Relationship of significant landscape features and surface treatments. The church sits directly on the wide sidewalks facing Russell. Foundation plantings and grass are present on the southeast side of the church and school between the building and the large asphalt parking lot. The parking lot abuts the building on its northeast end with no plated buffer. A concrete block wall with courses of yellow brick alternating every two blocks runs along the periphery of the parking lot on the northeast and southeast sides. On the northwest side of the church facing Service Street is a narrow grassy area between the sidewalk and the building. The sidewalk between the parking lot and church has a brownstone curb, as does the curb on Service Street. The parish house on Service Street has a small grassy lawn with minor plantings between it and the church.

(14) Relationship of open space to structures. Buildings either sit directly on wide sidewalks or the large parking lot or are separated by small planted strips of grass. The Service Street side of the district appears more closed-in due to the density and height of buildings along Gratiot Avenue, while the parking lot side with the green buffer results in a more spacious appearance on the southeast side facing Antietam.

(15) Scale of façades and façade elements. The scale of the church appears monumental due to the vertical emphasis and the visually dominant tower, although it is not an exceptionally large building. Elements within the façade are in keeping with the scale and style of the church. The parish house is small in scale and simple in detail; the school does not dominate on its own.

(16) Directional expression of front elevations. The directional expression of the church is emphatically vertical. The southwest and northwest elevations of the school are horizontal with neutralizing vertical elements, while the northeast end is neutral. The parish house is neutral in directional expression; verticality is emphasized by the frontal gable, but the chamfered wing balances the composition.

(17) Rhythm of building setbacks. Inapplicable due to single-complex district.

(18) Relationship of lot coverage. Inapplicable due to single-complex district.

(19) Degree of complexity within the façades. The placement and articulation of elements within the façades of the church, school and parish house are not complex, although the arrangement of masses and roofs of the parish house are complex.

(20) Orientation, vistas, overviews. The church is oriented towards Russell Street; the school is entered through its southeast side. The parish house is oriented towards Service Street. Due to the build-up of the frontage on Gratiot Avenue, the church can only be seen adequately from the northerly approach on Gratiot Avenue. The high wall partly blocks the view from Antietam, although glimpses of the corner tower can be had.

(21) Symmetric or asymmetric appearance. The Russell Street church façade is symmetrical in design with the exception of the two corner towers. The northeast end of the school is asymmetrical although balanced, and the parish house is asymmetrical although balanced.

(22) General environmental character. The church, school and parish house form a cohesive unit markedly different in character from the commercial, industrial and residential uses around them. Although the church complex is located off one of the City’s major arteries, it is partially hidden behind the built-up Gratiot Avenue frontage. The setting is very urban in character.

(e) In accordance with Section 21-2-76 of this Code, the Historic District Commission is authorized to consider interior features in certain portions of the St. John’s-St. Luke Evangelical Church located in the St. John’s-St. Luke Evangelical Church Historic District, and permits shall be required for such interior work in those portions of the St. John’s-St. Luke Evangelical Church, as provided for in Sections 21-2-71 through 21-2-81 of this Code, as if such work were exterior work:

(1) The interior spaces of the St. John’s-St. Luke Evangelical Church, which are hereby made subject to Historic District Commission consider-

CD21:81
§ 21-2-127

DETROIT CITY CODE

ation, are those spaces normally open to or seen by the public, including the nave, narthex, transepts, chancel, galleries and side aisles. Areas not open to and not ordinarily seen by the public, including sacristies, vesting rooms, basements, upper floors or attic areas, organ chambers, closets, service areas, and the entire interiors of the parish house and school, are not hereby made subject to Historic District Commission consideration. Areas made subject to Historic District Commission consideration are shown on the floor plan on file in the Office of the City Clerk, in the Office of the Historic Designation Advisory Board, and in the Office of the Historic District Commission.

(2) In considering proposals for the alteration, demolition, partial demolition, removal, or addition to any or all of the architectural features and permanent furnishings within the designated areas of the interior of the St. John’s-St. Luke Evangelical Church, the Historic District Commission shall use the following criteria:

a. Subsections (d)(1) through (22) of this section, as applicable;

b. The architectural or historical significance of the existing or proposed structure, feature, permanent furnishing, or fixture, and its relationship to the architectural and historical value of the St. John’s-St. Luke Evangelical Church Historic District;

c. The purpose of the designated spaces within the St. John’s-St. Luke Evangelical Church and the needs of its owners, provided, that such considerations shall not bind the Historic District Commission to permit any work solely on the basis of such considerations;

d. The provisions of Section 21-2-76 of this Code; and

e. Any other factor, including aesthetic, which the Historic District Commission deems to be pertinent.

(3) As a guide in considering proposals affecting the designated interior spaces of the St. John’s-St. Luke Evangelical Church, the Historic District Commission shall make use of a set of slides, taken by the staff of the Historic Designation Advisory Board prior to the effective date of this section, which was June 25, 1982,

and representing the state of those interior spaces as of the date of designation. Copies of this set of slides, together with a list describing each slide and a diagram showing the relationship of the slides to the designated interior spaces, are on file in the offices of the City Clerk, the Historic Designation Advisory Board, the Historic District Commission, and the Burton Historical Collection of the Detroit Public Library.

(Code 1964, § 28A-1-34; Code 1984, § 25-2-86; Ord. No. 507-H, § 1(28A-1-34), eff. 6-25-1982)

laws.title: Parker House Historic District
laws.content:
(a) An historic district to be known as the Parker House Historic District is hereby established in accordance with the provisions of this article.

(b) This historic district designation is hereby certified as being consistent with the Detroit Master Plan of Policies.

(c) The boundaries of the Parker House Historic District, as shown on the map on file in the Office of the City Clerk, are as follows:

(1) The center line of East Jefferson Avenue;

(2) The westerly line extended south of Lot 1, plat of that part of Claim No. 181, north of East Jefferson Avenue, for the heirs of Antoine Rivard, 1841, as subdivided into lots, as recorded in L 12, Pages 348, 349, 350, and 351 Deeds, WCR;

(3) The northerly line of said Lot 1; and

(4) The easterly line extended south of said Lot 1.

(These boundaries include Lot 1, plat of that part of Claim No. 181, north of East Jefferson Avenue, for the heirs of Antoine Rivard, 1841, as subdivided into lots, as recorded in L 12, Pages 348, 349, 350, and 351 Deeds, WCR.)

(d) The elements of design, as defined in Section 21-2-2 of this Code, shall be as follows:

(1) Height. The Parker House is $2\frac{1}{2}$ stories tall, meaning that it has two full stories and a third story within the roof.

(2) Proportion of building’s front façade. The building is slightly wider than tall from grade to the top of the gables.

(3) Proportion of openings within the façade. Openings comprise approximately 25 to 30 percent of the building’s front façade, including the windows in the gables and centrally placed dormer. Sash windows are emphatically taller than wide, as are the French doors over the entrance. The Tudor-arched entrance is surrounded by side lights and transom windows.

(4) Rhythm of solids and voids in front façade. Voids are arranged symmetrically within bays which subtly project or recede from the body of the building.

(5) Rhythm of spacing of buildings on street. Inapplicable due to single-building district.

(6) Rhythm of entrance and/or porch projections. Inapplicable due to single-building district.

(7) Relationship of materials. Kelly Island limestone is the primary material of the Parker House; Amherst sandstone is used as trim around the windows, entrance, and gables; sills and watercourse are also dressed in Amherst sandstone. Window trim, the dormer, and parapet rails are in wood. The original slate roof has been covered with asphalt shingles. The rear addition is common brick.

(8) Relationship of textures. The main material of the façade, the rock-faced course limestone with margins, contrasts with the smooth appearance of the sandstone trim. Wood trim also provides a smooth textural effect. The asphalt roof does not contribute to the textural interest of the building.

CD21:89
§ 21-2-130

DETROIT CITY CODE

(9) *Relationship of colors.* The limestone, sandstone trim, and mortar are light gray in color. The front door is a natural wood tone. The wood trim is painted white; window frames are painted black. The asphalt roof is black, contrasting to the overall light surface of the façade.

(10) *Relationship of architectural details.* Architectural details are architectonic. Hood moldings with label stops, corner blocks in window openings, the balcony railings, and the Tudor-arched entrance reflect the Gothic Revival idiom.

(11) *Relationship of roof shapes.* The main roof is hipped with a flat top. Shed dormers project from the sides; transverse roofs create two front gables. The roof of the addition to the rear appears flat.

(12) *Walls of continuity.* Inapplicable due to single-building district.

(13) *Relationship of significant landscape features and surface treatments.* Directly in front of the Parker House is a flat grass lawn. A brick sidewalk, which is immediately adjacent and parallel to the public sidewalk, is separated from the lawn by a low concrete retaining wall. A low brick and concrete planter is built into the brick wall. A straight concrete walk leads to the front porch; a concrete walk leads off to the side in each direction from the main walk. To the rear of the Parker House is a paved open area and a one-car width driveway to Larned Street.

(14) *Relationship of open space to structures.* The front lawn and the paved area in the rear are the only open spaces that relate to the structure. Buildings to the east and west are too close to create open space to the sides.

(15) *Scale of façade and façade elements.* The Parker House façade is that of a moderate-size residential building; elements within the façade are in scale with the façade. Tall windows, the use of rock-faced stone, and the spare use of ornament achieve a sense of monumentality of the building.

(16) *Direction expression in front elevation.* The front elevation of the Parker House is vertical in directional expression, due to the two projecting gables and elongated window openings.

(17) *Rhythm of building setbacks.* Inapplicable due to single-building district.

(18) *Relationship of lot coverages.* Inapplicable due to single-building district.

(19) *Degree of complexity within the façade.* The façade reflects a straightforward expression of the Gothic Revival style. It is not complex in the small number of ornamental elements and the arrangement of fenestration, although the various bays of the façade subtly recede or project.

(20) *Orientation, vistas, overviews.* The Parker House is oriented to the south towards East Jefferson Avenue and is directly across the street from the Sibley House. The Parker House is obscured when approached from East Jefferson Avenue because it is set back from the public right-of-way while the buildings to its sides are not.

(21) *Symmetric or asymmetric appearance.* The façade is not entirely symmetrical but results in a balanced and visually interesting composition.

(22) *General environmental character.* The character of the area around the Parker House is one of mixed usage, primarily commercial and institutional, housed in both older and more modern buildings. It is in the midst of a major transportation hub—the Chrysler Freeway is to the west and East Jefferson Avenue, a major east-west thoroughfare, is directly in front. The Parker House, located in a fast-paced, urban environment, remains as a vestige of East Jefferson Avenue’s past.

(Code 1964, § 28A-1-36; Code 1984, § 25-2-90; Ord. No. 536-H, § 1(28A-1-36), eff. 2-18-1983)

laws.content:
(a) An historic district to be known as the State Savings Bank Building Historic District is hereby established in accordance with the provisions of this article.

(b) This historic district designation is hereby certified as being consistent with the Detroit Master Plan of Policies.

(c) The boundaries of the State Savings Bank Building Historic District, as shown on the map on file in the Office of the City Clerk, are as follows:

On the north, the center line of Fort; on the south, the center line of Congress; on the west, the center line of Shelby; and on the east, the east line of Lot 14 on the south side of Fort Street, extended north, of the Military Reserve Subdivision (L5/P218), and the east line of Lot 15 on the north side of Congress; extended

CD21:96

laws.title: History
laws.content:
§ 21-2-133

south, of the Military Reserve Subdivision (L5/P218). This designation does not include the bridge which connects the State Savings Bank Building to the structure at 601 Shelby, and said bridge is hereby excluded from the designation of the State Savings Bank Building Historic District. The Historic District Commission shall review permits relating to said bridge only when said permits include work upon the State Savings Bank Building. (Legal description: Lots 13 and 14, South of Fort Street, and Lots 14 and 15, north of Congress Street, and vacated alley adjoining said lots, Military Reserve Subdivision as recorded in L5/P218 of Plats, WCR.)

(d) The elements of design, as defined in Section 21-2-2 of this Code, shall be as follows:

(1) *Height.* The State Savings Bank Building is a two-story space with a basement increasing in above-ground height at Congress Street. Thus, the Congress Street elevation is raised a full story above the sidewalk. Offices at the mezzanine level encircle the banking room but are not articulated on the exterior.

(2) *Proportion of buildings’ front façade.* The Fort Street (north) façade is approximately three times wider than tall to its cornice; the Congress Street (south) elevation is approximately $2\frac{1}{2}$ times wider than tall. The Shelby Street (west) elevation is considerably wider than it is tall. The dimensions of the building are 100 feet wide by 296 feet long.

(3) *Proportion of openings within the façade.* Openings in the Fort Street and Congress Street façades constitute approximately 33 percent of the façade and, above the basement level (above ground floor on Congress), openings are all taller than wide. At the ground level at Congress, the entrance opening and display windows are wider than tall. The Shelby Street elevation openings constitute approximately 50 percent. The basement facing Shelby is pierced with windows that increase in height and width as the height of the basement increases towards Congress, on which openings become display windows.

(4) *Rhythm of solids to voids in front façade.* The Fort Street and Congress Street elevations are articulated in three bays. The central bay of the Fort Street façade contains a portico in antis with a recessed entrance flanked by two monu-

mentally treated round-headed windows. The Congress Street face contains three such windows and has storefront windows and an entrance in the granite base. The Shelby Street elevation is composed of 11 bays of colossal round-arched fenestration; its middle bay is set apart from its flanking bays by rusticated masonry piers and two stacked rectangular windows. A window punctures the base beneath each monumental window, progressively increasing in height and width towards Congress Street. Voids throughout are arranged symmetrically.

(5) *Rhythm of spacing of buildings on street.* Inapplicable due to single-building district.

(6) *Rhythm of entrance and/or porch projections.* Inapplicable due to single-building district.

(7) *Relationship of materials.* Marble is the major material of the State Savings Bank Building; its base is granite. The remodeled entrance wall within the Fort Street portico is faced with polished marble surrounding a glass and aluminum door unit. The base on Congress and Shelby is punctured with plate glass windows shielded by metal grills excepting the shop windows. The arched windows are fitted with bronze window units; the arches of the windows are wood. Cloth awnings provide shelter above the windows and entrance along Congress Street.

(8) *Relationship of textures.* Regular blocks of smooth marble facing contrasts with the rusticated corner and dividing piers. The entrance wall is polished marble; the foundations are unpolished granite. Detailing, such as the modillion cornice, the fluted columns and the balustrade, contribute to the textural effect.

(9) *Relationship of color.* White is the color of the main body of the building; the base is pink-gray. The bronze window infill is now painted black. The remodeled entrance wall is polished black and red marble.

(10) *Relationship of architectural details.* Details are in the Beaux Arts classical mode. The main feature of the front (Fort Street) façade is the Ionic portico in antis flanked by monumentally treated round-headed fenestration. These tripartite window units containing two levels of sash are set within marble arches with keystones. The portico, with two freestanding fluted monolithic Ionic columns, shelters the modern-style

main entrance. Above the portico and modil-
lion cornice and attic, a freestanding classical
sculptural group caps the parapet wall. It is
composed of a pair of classically draped female
figures representing industry and commerce
flanking a scrolled cartouche, cornucopias, and

laws.title: St. Josaphat Historic District
laws.content:
(a) An historic district to be known as the St. Josaphat Historic District is hereby established in accordance with the provisions of this article.

(b) The historic district designation is hereby certified as being consistent with the Detroit Master Plan of Policies.

(c) The boundaries of the St. Josaphat Historic District, as shown on the map on file in the Office of the City Clerk, are as follows:

On the east, the Chrysler Service Drive; on the south, the center line of Canfield; on the north, the center line of St. Josaphat alley (vacated); and on the west, the west line of Lot 7 of C. Moran’s Sub. of C. Moran Farm. (The property included within these boundaries consists of C. Moran’s Subdivision of the C. Moran Farm. Lots 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7, Detroit, Michigan (L3/P73); and Zoltowski’s Subdivision of Lots 1 and 2, north side of Fremont Street, C. Moran Farm, Detroit, Michigan, Lots 1-5 (L12/P84).)

(d) The elements of design, as defined in Section 21-2-2 of this Code, shall be as follows:

(1) **Height.** St. Josaphat Roman Catholic Church is a tall single-story space with a central tower approximately 200 feet in height. Its two corner towers are approximately 100 feet high. The sisters’ house and the rectory are 2½-story buildings, and the boiler house/caretaker’s residence is one to 1½ stories in height.

(2) **Proportion of buildings’ front façades.** The front façade of St. Josaphat Roman Catholic Church is emphatically taller than wide, the central tower being the dominant vertical element. The sisters’ house and rectory are wider than tall to their eaves but are just as wide as tall to the top of their roofs. The boiler house/caretaker’s residence forms a unit substantially wider than tall. The church building is the predominant building in the parish complex. The three ancillary buildings are compatible with one another in the proportions of their front elevations.

(3) **Proportion of openings with the façades.** Openings in the main (south) façade of the church constitute approximately ten to 15 percent. The secondary façade, along the Chrysler Freeway Service Drive, is fenestrated with large round-headed window openings and a rose window in the transept arm. All window and door openings of the church are taller than wide; the exception being the round windows in the towers and rose windows in the transept. The façade of the sisters’ house and the rectory are each composed of 20 to 30 percent openings, all taller than wide, with the exception of the basement windows in the sisters’ house, which are wider than tall. The boiler house has no windows but does have a two-car garage opening in its front elevation; its caretaker’s section has approximately 20 percent openings.

(4) **Rhythm of solids to voids in front façades.** The main (south) façade of the church is divided into three projecting vertical sections: a central bell tower and two side towers. Voids are arranged symmetrically, the two corner towers being identically fenestrated. Each tower contains a large round-headed arched entrance. Above the entrance of the central tower is a large three-part opening consisting of elongated round-headed stained glass windows. Above this is a round window. In the second stage of the central tower are two elongated arched openings with small rectangular louvered openings in the turrets. The top stage of the central tower, beneath the spire, contains paired round arched louvered openings. Above the entrance of each of the corner towers is a pair of smaller rectangular window openings with a round window above. Their top stages contain two louvered round-headed windows. The main feature of the east elevation along Chrysler Freeway Service Drive is the rose window in the transept arm. All side aisle, chapel, and altar windows along the east elevation also have round arches. Centrally placed entrances exist on the sisters’ house, rectory, and caretaker’s residence. Most windows are two times taller than wide and are evenly and symmetrically placed. Dormers project from both the sisters’ house and rectory. The most prominent void in the rectory is the large arched window on the second-story level on the west side of the building.

(5) **Rhythm of spacing of buildings on street.** Inapplicable due to single-complex district.

(6) **Rhythm of entrance and/or porch projection.** Inapplicable due to single-complex district.

CD21:101
§ 21-2-135

DETROIT CITY CODE

(7) *Relationship of materials.* The main material of the church and other three buildings included in the district is brick. It is contrasted with steps, foundations, watercourses, stringcourses, and trim of Bedford limestone and window frames and/or sashes of wood. The church spires are covered with slate, and the side aisles of the church are covered in copper. All other roof areas are covered in asphalt shingles. The porches of the rectory and boiler house/caretaker’s residence are wood; dormers are also of wood.

(8) *Relationship of textures.* Rough-cut limestone foundations and smooth limestone water tables, stringcourses, and trim provide contrast with the brick with plain-cut mortar joints. Wooden trim and sash of the sisters’ house, rectory and boiler house/caretaker’s residence also provide contrast with the brick. Slate-covered spires and copper-covered side aisles of the church contribute greatly to the textural interest; asphalt shingles generally do not. Stained glass windows in the church contribute to the textural effect.

(9) *Relationship of color.* The light gray limestone contrasts with the orange brick. Wood trim and architectural elements, such as the fleche of the church and porch on the rectory, are painted white. The spires of the church are clad in gray slate; the copper roofing over the side aisles is green. All other roofing material in the district is black asphalt. Crosses at the pinnacles of the three church towers are gilded. Doors of the church and rectory are natural oak in color; the doors of the sisters’ house and boiler house/caretaker’s residence are painted white. The church, boiler house and rectory have reddish-brown gutters; the sisters’ house has white gutters and downspouts.

(10) *Relationship of architectural details.* Victorian Romanesque Ecclesiastical architectural details accentuate the church structure. The façade is dominated by a large central tower which is flanked by twin-buttressed towers containing secondary entrances. The round arch motif is repeated in the enriched arches of the portals and the arcade fenestration throughout the building. Buttresses are frequently capped with stone trim and gabled projections. Pinnacles at the corners of the towers culminate in finials, and the spires carry crosses. Blind arcading and brick circles ornament the spaces beneath transitional stages of the towers, beneath the eaves of the central spire, and under the eaves of the nave roof. Stone strapwork and trim unify the architectural elements. Stained glass windows are discernible from the exterior. The paired ionic columns of the porch are the major architectural elements of the rectory. This porch extends along the façade to the east two-story bay window with conical roof above. Stone stringcourses and wooden eave brackets are visible on the rectory and sisters’ house. A blind oculus with keystones at each compass point ornaments the west bay of the sisters’ house. The one-story boiler house has a corbelled cornice line; the caretaker’s residence bears little ornamental detail.

(11) *Relationship of roof shapes.* St. Josaphat Roman Catholic Church has a pitched roof over the nave flanked by lower aisles. A transverse gable roof intersects the nave, resulting in the transept; a fleche rises from the roof ridge at the transept crossing. Octagonal spires and pinnacles project from the three towers. The boiler house has a flat roof not visible from the street; its attached caretaker’s residence and the sisters’ house have steeply hipped roofs. The rectory has intersecting hipped roofs and a conical roof over the east bay.

(12) *Walls of continuity.* Inapplicable due to single-complex district.

(13) *Relationship of significant landscape features and surface treatments.* The church sits directly on the concrete sidewalk. Grassy areas exist along the east elevation to the sides of the projecting transept arms. A black wrought iron fence extends westward along the front property line from the church to the western property line of the parish, then along the western property line along the side of the sisters’ house. It also extends along the east side of the parking lot to the church’s rear yard. A chain-linked fence separates the church complex from the land to the north. Flat lawns exist in front of the sisters’ house and rectory; the rectory has small side yards. A large asphalt parking lot is located between the rectory and sisters’ house and extends northward. The boiler house/caretaker’s residence fronts on the parking lot. In the rear yard of the church are concrete walkways, a

CD21:102

laws.title: History
laws.content:
§ 21-2-135

patio, and flower gardens. Deciduous and evergreen plantings exist on the rectory site and the church’s rear yard.

(14) *Relationship of open space to structures.* Open space to the sidewalk exists in front of the church, and in the form of small grass turf areas between the church and the sidewalk to the east of the church. Behind the church is an ample landscaped rear yard. A large parking lot is situated between the rectory and the sisters’ house; the boiler house/caretaker’s residence fronts on the northeast corner of the parking lot. There are small lawns between the public sidewalk along East Canfield and the sisters’ house and rectory, and the rectory has a small side yard on its west side. The sisters’ house abuts the parking lot on its east side.

(15) *Scale of façade and façade elements.* The scale of St. Josaphat Roman Catholic Church is monumental. Its triple-towered façade contributes greatly to its overall monumental effect, as do the elongated windows and moderately sized details within the composition. The rectory and sisters’ house are on the scale of residences of moderate size, while the boiler house/caretaker’s residence is small in scale. Details within the three ancillary buildings are few; they are restrained and small in scale.

(16) *Directional expression of front elevation.* The directional expression of the church is emphatically vertical, verticality being emphasized by the three towers. The sisters’ house and rectory are slightly wider than tall to their eaves but their steeply sloped roofs neutralize their directional expression. The boiler house/caretaker’s residence is horizontal in directional expression.

(17) *Rhythm of building setbacks.* The sisters’ house and rectory are set back approximately similar distances from the public sidewalk; they are not related to the setback of the church. The boiler house/caretaker’s residence is at the rear of the site.

(18) *Relationship of lot coverages.* The buildings occupy the perimeter of the site, the boiler house/caretaker’s residence being at the rear, or north end of the site, and the other fronting on East Canfield. The parking lot occupies a large portion of the frontage on East Canfield and the center of the site.

(19) *Degree of complexity within the façades.* The façade of the church is symmetrical, yet complex in its use of extensive Victorian Romanesque vocabulary. The façades of the sisters’ house and rectory are somewhat complex in their massing. Both are composed of three bays. The sisters’ house is bowed on its west bay and the rectory bows out on its east bay. The façade of the boiler house/caretaker’s residence is not complex.

(20) *Orientation, vistas, overviews.* The complex of buildings is oriented towards the south, or East Canfield Street. The boiler house/caretaker’s residence is entered off the parking lot or concrete walk extending north from the rectory. The church, and its spires in particular, provide a landmark from all directions at a distance.

(21) *Symmetric or asymmetric appearance.* St. Josaphat Roman Catholic Church is symmetrical in appearance. The rectory and sisters’ house are asymmetrical, although they are each balanced architectural compositions. The caretaker’s residence is symmetrical with the exception of its basement openings; however, together with the attached boiler house, it forms an asymmetrical arrangement.

(22) *General environmental character.* St. Josaphat Roman Catholic Parish is a very visible special use element in the residential redevelopment area immediately surrounding it and the medical center redevelopment area in general. It is the westernmost of three monumental historic Polish Catholic Churches within one-half mile of each other along East Canfield Street, providing a visible reminder of the historic ethnic ties of this area of the City.

(e) In accordance with Section 21-2-76 of this Code, the Historic District Commission is hereby authorized to consider interior features in certain portions of St. Josaphat Roman Catholic Church, located in the St. Josaphat Historic District, and permits shall be required for such interior work in those portions of the St. Josaphat Church as provided for in Section 21-2-71 of this Code, as if such work were exterior work:

(1) The interior spaces of St. Josaphat Roman Catholic Church, which are hereby made subject to the Historic District Commission’s consideration, are those spaces normally open to or seen by the public, including the nave, narthex, tran-

CD21:103
$\S 21-2-135$

DETROIT CITY CODE

septs, chancel, chapels, galleries, and side aisles. Areas not open to and not ordinarily seen by the public, including the sacristies, vesting rooms, basements, upper floors or attic areas, organ chambers, closets, service areas, and the entire interiors of the sisters' house, rectory and boiler house/caretaker's residence are not hereby made subject to Historic District Commission consideration. Areas made subject to Historic District Commission consideration are shown on the floor plan on file in the Office of the City Clerk, in the Office of the Historic Designation Advisory Board, and in the Office of the Historic District Commission.

(2) In considering proposals for the alteration, demolition, partial demolition, removal, or addition to any or all of the architectural features and permanent furnishings within the designated areas of the interior of St. Josaphat Roman Catholic Church, the Historic District Commission shall use the following criteria:

a. Subsections (e)(1) through (22) of this section as applicable;

b. The architectural or historical significance of the existing or proposed structure, feature, permanent furnishing, or fixture, and its relationship to the architectural and historical value of the St. Josaphat Historic District;

c. The purpose of the designated spaces within the St. Josaphat Roman Catholic Church and the needs of its owners, provided, that such consideration shall not bind the Historic District Commission to permit any work solely on the basis of such considerations;

d. The provisions of Section 21-2-76 of this Code;

e. Any other factor, including aesthetic, which the Historic District Commission deems to be pertinent.

(3) As a guide in considering any proposal affecting the designated interior spaces of the St. Josaphat Roman Catholic Church, the Historic District Commission shall make use of a set of slides, which were taken by the staff of the Historic Designation Advisory Board prior to December 16, 1983, and represent the state of those interior spaces as of the date of designation.

Copies of this set of slides, together with a list describing each slide and a diagram showing the relationship of the slides to the designated interior spaces, are on file in the Offices of the City Clerk, the Historic Designation Advisory Board, the Historic District Commission, and the Burton Historical Collection of the Detroit Public Library.

(Code 1964, § 28A-1-42; Code 1984, § 25-2-93; Ord. No. 574-H, § 1(28A-1-42), eff. 12-16-1983)

laws.title: Frank H. Beard School Historic District
laws.content:
(a) An historic district to be known as the Frank H. Beard School Historic District is hereby established in accordance with the provisions of this article.

(b) This historic district designation is hereby certified as being consistent with the Detroit Master Plan of Policies.

(c) The boundaries of the Frank H. Beard School Historic District, as shown on the map on file in the Office of the City Clerk, are as follows:

On the north, the center line of West Lafayette Boulevard; on the east, the center line of an alley running north-south between Rademacher and Waterman from West Lafayette Boulevard to the Fisher Freeway Service Drive; on the south, the center line of Fisher Freeway Service Drive; and on the west, the center line of Waterman Avenue. (These boundaries include the triangular part of Lot 46 being north 21.84 feet on the east line and east 151.23 feet on the north line, Kaiers Sub, L27 P14; and Lots 12-15, Cynthia W. Crawford’s Sub, L4/P47, except the triangular part being west 6.27 feet on the south line and south 37.01 feet on the west line.)

(d) The elements of design, as defined in Section 21-2-2 of this Code, shall be as follows:

(1) Height. The building is two stories tall to the eaves of the roof, or approximately 36 feet in height, including the high basement. The central tower is approximately 55 feet in height.

(2) Proportion of building’s front façade. Frank H. Beard School is wider than tall. The symmetrical façade is composed of five bays, the end bays being the widest, and the central entrance bay being the narrowest.

(3) Proportion of openings within the façade. The double-hung sash windows, with transom windows above on the first and second stories of the front façade, are $2\frac{1}{2}$ times taller than wide. The double-hung sash basement windows are also taller than wide. The central bay contains a large rounded arched entrance. Above this are two half-round window openings. At the second-story level in the central bay are a pair of double-hung sash windows with transoms above, and above these, at attic level, are a pair of double-hung sash windows with half-round transom windows. The top stage of the tower contains an almost square opening. A gable with a single round arched double-hung sash window projects from the bays that flank the central tower. Overall, the front façade consists of approximately 20 percent voids.

(4) Rhythm of solids to voids in front façade. A symmetrical grid pattern is clearly discernible on the front façade, as well as the north and south elevations. Fenestration within the five bays of the front façade is rhythmically arranged; there are rows of four windows within the two outer bays, rows of three windows in the bay flanking the central bay, and a pair of windows in the central entrance bay. A rhythm of three windows, two windows, and four windows from front to back exists on the side elevations.

(5) Rhythm of spacing of buildings on street. Inapplicable due to single-building district.

(6) Rhythm of entrance and/or porch projections. Inapplicable due to single-building district.

(7) Relationship of materials. The major material of the building is brick. Sills and stringcourses are stone, as are the pier capitals in the entrance and the porch steps. There is a stone panel with the name "Frank H. Beard School" carved into it above the entrance. The cornice above this insignia is pressed metal. Wooden sash windows are recessed in wooden window frames. The roof is asphalt shingles.

(8) Relationship of textures. Many different textural effects are created by the type, the treatment,

CD21:107
§ 21-2-137

DETROIT CITY CODE

and the juxtaposition of materials. The major textural effect is that created by the coursed brick, now smoothened by its painted surface, contrasted with the smooth wooden sash and window frames and rough-faced and smooth stone. At the basement and first-story levels, every fifth row of brick protrudes and every other voussoir above the windows protrudes, creating a texture that results in a rusticated appearance. Rough-cut stone sills, raised brick belt courses, decorative brickwood, carved stone, and pressed metal contribute greatly to textural interest. The asphalt roof generally does not contribute to textural interest.

(9) Relationship of colors. The orange-red brick building is now painted light blue-gray, as is most of the stonework of the building and the pressed metal above the entrance. The entrance arch and double doors of the entrance are painted a darker shade of blue-gray. The wooden window frames, sash and cornice are painted white, and the roof is black.

(10) Relationship of architectural details. The details of the building are Victorian Romanesque in style. Symmetrical in arrangement, the front façade is organized into five bays. Its two end bays and central bay project outward while two recede. The central bay extends upward, culminating in an open tower with a pyramidal roof. A wide stubby pier with a Medieval stone capital bearing floral and grotesque motifs flanks each side of the arched entrance. The large entry arch has a keystone in its center. Two round panels, one on each side of the arched entrance, bear no ornamentation. Above the arch is a horizontal stone panel with the inscription "Frank H. Beard School." The cornice above the insignia bears an egg and dart pattern. Semi-circular arched windows above the cornice have pronounced brick voussoirs. In carved brick panels between the second and third stages of the tower are the inscriptions "1886" and "1896." To either side of the central tower is a steeply pitched dormer; the gables have flared ends and are crowned by finials. There are continuous stone window sills, molded bricks framing the window openings, and a molded brick belt course between the first and the second story. At the basement and first-story levels, every fifth row of brick protrudes and every other voussoir

above the window protrudes, resulting in a rusticated appearance. The side elevations are comprised of similar moldings and continuous belt courses and stone sills. The rear of the building is plain; it contains no decorative brick but does have non-continuous stone sills.

(11) Relationship of roof shapes. The roof of Beard School is comprised of a number of shallow hips. The frontal dormers have steeply pitched roofs, and the tower has a pyramidal roof over it.

(12) Walls of continuity. Inapplicable due to single-building district.

(13) Relationship of significant landscape features and surface treatments. The school building fronts on a shallow grass turf lawn planted with a few scattered trees and deciduous bushes around the entrance. A straight concrete walk leads from the public sidewalk to the front steps of the building. A straight sidewalk from the public sidewalk leads to the rear of the building on its south side. At the rear of the school, there is a grass turf between the school and the north-south concrete alley that runs parallel to the school. On the north side is a chain-link fenced play area. There is a playground and a gravel parking lot to the rear, or east, of the district.

(14) Relationship of open space to structure. Open space exists to the front, sides, and rear of the school building in the form of shallow grassy lawns divided by concrete walks.

(15) Scale of façade and façade elements. The façade is large in scale, with some large elements, such as the tower and entrance arch. There are smaller elements within the composition.

(16) Directional expression of front elevation. Although the directional expression of the building is horizontal because the building is considerably longer than tall, vertical elements, such as tower and two dormers, create vertical thrusts.

(17) Rhythm of building setbacks. Inapplicable due to single-building district.

(18) Relationship of lot coverages. Inapplicable due to single-building district.

(19) Degree of complexity within the façade. The façade exhibits a straightforward representation

laws.title: Croul-Palms House Historic District
laws.content:
(a) An historic district to be known as the Croul-Palms House Historic District is hereby established in accordance with the provisions of this article.

(b) This historic district designation is hereby certified as being consistent with the Detroit Master Plan of Policies.

(c) The boundaries of the Croul-Palms House Historic District, as shown on the map on file in the Office of the City Clerk, are as follows:

All that portion of the Mullett Farm lying between the southerly line of East Jefferson Avenue and the northerly line of Woodbridge Street bounded as follows: Beginning at a point on the southerly line of East Jefferson Avenue 7.10 feet on course south 60 degrees west from point of intersection of the southerly line of East Jefferson Avenue and the westerly line of Guoin Farm; thence southerly 200.48 feet to a point on the northerly line of Woodbridge Street, said point being situated south 60 degrees west 3.30 feet from the dividing line between Guoin and Mullett Farm; thence south 60 degrees west along said northerly line of Woodbridge Street 70 feet to the easterly line of Lot 4 on Mullett Farm, as designated on recent map of the City; thence north 26 degrees west along the line of said Lot 4, 200.48 feet to the southerly line of East Jefferson Avenue; thence north 60 degrees east along the said southerly line East Jefferson Avenue 66.20 feet to the place of beginning, said premises being a portion of Lot 3 Mullett Farm, between East Jefferson Avenue and Woodbridge Street, Wayne County, Michigan. Given to correct description in Deed L. 3707, P. 423; also including that part of East Jefferson Avenue 120 feet wide being the southern half of East Jefferson Avenue adjacent to the above-described property.

(d) The elements of design, as defined in Section 21-2-2 of this Code, shall be as follows:

(1) Height. The Croul-Palms House is $2\frac{1}{2}$ stories tall, with a full story contained in the roof.

(2) Proportion of building’s front façade. While the façade is slightly wider than it is tall to the eaves of the roof, the division of the façade into three vertical sections and the treatment of the roof above the wall creates a vertical proportional system.

(3) Proportion of openings within the façade. Windows and doors amount to approximately 25 percent of the front façade area, including openings in the roof projections. All window and door openings are taller than wide, except the basement windows, which are square, and the segmentally arched transom over the entrance. All windows on the front façade are one-over-one sash, except the basement windows in the western bay which contain single panes.

(4) Rhythm of solids to voids in front façade. The three sections of the front façade are each fenestrated within themselves. The western section rising through three stories contains a three-sided bay with elongated double-hung sash windows, one per face of the bay. The windows in the projecting gable of the dormer are shorter in height than those in the first and second story. The central section consists of an elaborate recessed entryway with ornate double doors and segmentally arched transom window above. Above this entrance at the second-story level is a centered double-hung sash window; and above it, projecting from the roof, is a gabled dormer with a double-hung sash window. The three-story bank of windows angled to the northeast corner of the building comprises the east bay. It is pierced with two elongated window openings

on the frontal surface of the bay and one identical double-hung sash window per each side of the bay on the first and second stories, and one double-hung sash window in the frontal surface of the third story, within the gable. The top sashes of the windows on the first story are only one-half the height of the lower sashes. In general, the arrangement of solids to voids in the front façade is very rhythmic, and is dictated by the different surface planes.

(5) *Rhythm of spacing of buildings on streets.* Inapplicable due to single-building district.

(6) *Rhythm of entrance or porch projections.* Inapplicable due to single-building district.

(7) *Relationship of materials.* Brick is the major material of the building; limestone is the secondary material. Limestone is used for the foundations, steps, sills and belt courses. Wood is used for window frames, sashes, cornices, gable ends, and decorative trim. The front double doors and jambs are maple. The roof is covered in asphalt shingles. Gutters, downspouts and roof ridge cresting on the front façade, and roof section of the house, are copper.

(8) *Relationship of textures.* The pressed brick with then recessed mortar joints contrasts with the rock-faced margined stone foundations and smooth stone trim. The wood surfaces are also smooth in texture. Textural interest is created when the wood contains decorative carving. The asphalt shingles of the roof do not contribute to textural interest.

(9) *Relationship to color.* The major color relationship is that of red brick contrasting with light gray stone foundations and belt courses. Mortar between the closely laid bricks is gray with multi-colored aggregate and is not very visible. The mortar between the stones of the foundations matches the light gray stone. All wood is painted cream color. The asphalt roof is black. Copper gutters, downspouts, and cresting along roof ridges, which can be seen from the front, or north, are now brown but will weather to green. The double doors of the entrance are finished natural maple.

(10) *Relationship of architectural details.* Much of the detail on the Queen Anne-style building is carried out in wood or stone; wooden gable panels, segmentally arched panels above win-

dows, and vergeboards are carved in floral motifs. Pendants hang from the ends of the vergeboards and eave brackets support the overhang of the roof. A simple wooden cornice divides the roof from the wall. The low stone walls of the porch flair outward at the base; a canvas awning in the hipped shape of the original porch roof is supported on black metal tubular columns. The paneled wooden double doors are ornately carved with floral motifs. Incised geometric and floral details also appear in corners and between windows on the stone belt courses. Belt courses continue up and over the tops of the windows; window sills form a portion of continuous belt courses.

(11) *Relationship of roof shapes.* The basic roof form is a hip roof with a flat center. There are subsidiary gable roofs extended into dormers and subsidiary hip roofs. The gabled dormer on the northeast corner faces the corner; the gabled dormer of the west bay faces north, or front, as does the gable of the smaller central gable.

(12) *Walls of continuity.* Inapplicable due to single-building district.

(13) *Relationship of significant landscape features and surface treatments.* The front yard is composed of ground cover behind a wood tie retaining wall separating it from the public sidewalk. The front yard is approximately 18 inches above the grade of the public sidewalk. Two steps lead from the public sidewalk to a brick-paved circular surface with a light pole in the center. This brick wall leads to the stone front steps to the porch of the house. A straight-line driveway along the west side of the house, where originally there was an ornate porch, leads to a paved asphalt parking lot in the back of the lot. A small porch with handicap ramp is located on the recessed east side of the rear elevation of the house.

(14) *Relationship of open space to structure.* The front of the house faces onto a shallow front yard. There is a very narrow grassy side yard between the Croul-Palms House and the apartment building to the east. To the west is a straight driveway leading to an asphalt parking lot in the rear. laws.title: Atkinson Avenue Historic District
laws.content:
(a) An historic district to be known as the Atkinson Avenue Historic District is hereby established in accordance with the provisions of this article.

(b) This historic district designation is hereby certified as being consistent with the Detroit Master Plan of Policies.

(c) The boundaries of the Atkinson Avenue Historic District, as shown on the map on file in the Office of the City Clerk, are as follows:

On the north, the alley between Atkinson and Edison; on the east, the center line of the John C. Lodge service drive; on the south, the alley between Atkinson and Clairmount; and on the west, the center line of Linwood. (These boundaries include Lots 561 to 682, Joy Farm Sub (L32/P39 and 40); Lots 1-16, Lewis Park Sub (L30/P96); Lots 1-16, Jackson Park Sub (L30/P95); Lots 1-72, Boston Boulevard Sub (L29/P23); and Lots 1-16, Guerold’s Sub (L29/P87).)

(d) The elements of design, as defined in Section 21-2-2 of this Code, shall be as follows:

(1) *Height.* Virtually all the houses in the district have two full stories plus an attic or finished third floor within the roof; these are generally called "two-and-a-half" story houses. Some two-story two-flat buildings on the 1600 block of Atkinson between Woodrow Wilson and Rosa Parks Boulevard are slightly taller in height than the single-family residences. The commercial row on Rosa Parks is two stories tall with a flat roof; the church building on Rosa Parks is also two stories in height.

(2) *Proportion of buildings’ front façades.* Proportion varies in the district, depending on age, style, and location within a specific subdivision. Most houses are slightly wider than tall or as wide as tall, excluding the roof. Exceptions occur primarily on corner lots where the houses that face the north-south street are wider than tall. The commercial row on the southeast corner of Rosa Parks is wider than tall.

CD21:111
§ 21-2-139

DETROIT CITY CODE

(3) Proportion of openings within the façades. Window openings are almost always taller than wide; several windows are sometimes grouped into combinations wider than tall. Window openings are always subdivided, the most common window type being double-hung sash, whose area is sometimes further subdivided by muntins. Façades have approximately 15 to 35 percent of their area glazed. Dormer windows exist in a variety of shapes and sizes.

(4) Rhythm of solids to voids in front façades. In buildings derived from Classical traditions, voids are usually arranged in a symmetrical and evenly-spaced manner within the façades. In examples of other styles, particularly those of English Medieval inspiration, voids are arranged with more freedom but usually result in balanced compositions.

(5) Rhythm of spacing of buildings on street. The spacing of buildings on Atkinson Avenue is generally determined by the setback from the side lot lines. There is little variance in the size of lots on Atkinson between the Lodge Freeway Service Drive and Linwood; lots average 35 to 40 feet wide. Most buildings are centered on their lots and are at least four feet from the side lot lines as required by subdivision restrictions, with little or no side yards. Many properties have narrow driveways along the side lot line.

(6) Rhythm of entrance and/or porch projections. Most buildings in the district have entrance and/or porch projections facing the street, creating a rhythm where they exist in numbers. In those buildings of classical inspiration, porches and entrances tend to be centered on the front façades. Other stylistic examples display more freedom in entrance and front-porch placement. A few houses have front porches extending to the sides of the building; some houses have their major entrances on the side of the building. The multi-unit buildings between Woodrow Wilson and Rosa Parks Boulevard frequently have second-story porches above the first-story porches. Many porches, particularly those in the western half of the district have metal or cloth awnings.

(7) Relationship of materials. The major building materials in the district are brick and stucco, sometimes used in combination, wooden functional trim and window frames and sash are common, and wood is used in many examples as decorative trim as well. Wood sheathing is occasionally used on the attic story and/or dormers. Stone is occasionally used as a material for window sills, porch trim, and other functional trim. Rough-cut stone is the main material used on a rustic porch in the district. Roofing materials include asphalt shingles, slate, and Mediterranean tiles, asphalt shingles being by far the primary roofing material in the district.

(8) Relationship of textures. The most common relationship of textures in the district is that of low-relief pattern of mortar joints in brick contrasted with the smooth surface of wood or stone trim. Stuccoed surfaces contrast with brick when used in combination and with wood or stone trim. Half-timbering on Neo-Tudor buildings creates textural interest. Tile and slate roofs have particular textural interest where they exist, whereas asphalt shingles generally do not.

(9) Relationship of colors. Natural brick colors (red, yellow, brown, buff) predominate on wall surfaces. Where stucco and concrete exists, it is usually left in its natural state or painted in a shade of cream. Asphalt-shingled roofs are predominantly in natural colors (tile and slate colors), and in appropriate lighter colors. Paint colors often relate to style; the Classically-inspired buildings generally have woodwork painted in the white and cream range. Doors and shutters feature an array of colors, usually harmonizing with the main body of the house. Colors known to have been in use on buildings of this type in the 18th Century or early 19th Century on similar buildings may be considered for suitability. Buildings of Medieval or Craftsman inspiration generally have painted woodwork and window frames of dark brown, cream, or other natural tones. Original color schemes for any given building may be determined by professional paint analysis and, when so determined, are always appropriate for that building and may provide suggestion for similar houses.

(10) Relationship of architectural detail. These generally relate to style; Neo-Georgian and Colonial Revival buildings display classical details, mostly in wood. Areas commonly, but not always, treated are porches, shutters, window frames, cornices, and dormer windows. Details on Mediterra-

laws.content:
(a) An historic district to be known as the Peterboro-Charlotte Historic District is hereby established in accordance with the provisions of this article.

(b) This historic district designation is hereby certified as being consistent with the Detroit Master Plan of Policies.

(c) The boundaries of the Peterboro-Charlotte Historic District, as shown on the map on file in the Office of the City Clerk, are as follows:

On the north, the center line of Peterboro; on the west, the center line of Park; on the south, the center line of Charlotte; and on the east, the center line of Woodward Avenue. (d) The elements of design, as defined in Section 21-2-2 of this Code, shall be as follows:

(1) *Height.* All of the primary buildings in the district are between one and six stories tall. All houses are either two or $2\frac{1}{2}$ stories in height and the Addison Hotel at 14 Charlotte is six stories in height. Three of the four commercial buildings on Woodward Avenue are two stories tall; the former service station building is one story.

(2) *Proportion of buildings’ front façades.* Most of the residential buildings in the district are taller than wide, with the exceptions being the Scott Mansion at 81 Peterboro, the building at 3126 Park, and the Addison Hotel at 14 Charlotte, which are wider than tall. The commercial buildings facing Woodward Avenue are wider than tall, and taken together, form a continuous building wall substantially wider than tall.

(3) *Proportion of openings within the façades.* Areas of voids generally constitute approximately 30 percent of the front façades of the small-scale residential structures, excluding the roofs, and between 20 percent and 35 percent of the front façades of the larger multi-unit residential structures. Most window openings in residential buildings are taller than wide, although when grouped together, openings may achieve a horizontal effect. Transoms are wider than tall or square. Window openings are frequently present in gables, turrets, and/or foundations. A great variety of sizes, shapes, and arrangements of openings exist among the residential buildings in the district. The four commercial buildings on Woodward Avenue have large storefront openings and, where a second story exists, second story openings that are wider than tall. laws.title: Chalfonte Apartments Historic District
laws.content:
(a) An historic district to be known as the Chalfonte Apartments Historic District is hereby established in accordance with the provisions of this article.

(b) This historic district designation is hereby certified as being consistent with the Detroit Master Plan of Policies.

(c) The boundaries of the Chalfonte Apartments Historic District, as shown on the map on file in the Office of the City Clerk, are as follows:

On the south, the center line of East Jefferson Avenue; on the east, the center line of Fischer Avenue; on the north, the center line of the east-west alley lying between East Jefferson Avenue and Agnes; and on the west, the eastern boundary of the Park Sub of the Cook Farm (L19/P59). (The property enclosed within these boundaries includes Lot B of Bernhart and Fischer’s Sub (L10/P27).)

(d) The elements of design, as defined in Section 21-2-2 of this Code, shall be as follows:

(1) *Height.* All three buildings are of identical height, three stories on a tall basement.

(2) *Proportion of buildings’ front façades.* Because the two buildings facing East Jefferson Avenue share a party wall, their façades join to form a single unit much wider than tall; the porches and bay windows centered on each building break up the horizontal expanse and neutralize the horizontal expression to a considerable extent. The building facing Fischer is approximately as wide as it is tall, and the bay windows provide vertically to the composition.

(3) *Proportion of openings within the façades.* All individual openings are taller than wide, although paired windows creating a unit approximately square are common, and the main entrance doorways are widened with sidelights. Overall, the façades are about 26 percent voids.

(4) *Rhythm of solids to voids in front façades.* The rhythm of solids to voids in all three buildings is identical. Openings are grouped in five vertical bays, with paired double-hung sash in the outer and center bays, and entrance doors on the first floor of the center bay. Single double-hung windows in each of the three faces of the intermediate bays, made up of bay windows extending from the ground level to the parapet.

CD21:125
§ 21-2-143

DETROIT CITY CODE

(5) *Rhythm of spacing of buildings on street.* Inapplicable, since no rhythm is established; the two buildings facing on East Jefferson Avenue are attached at a party wall, and only one building faces on Fischer.

(6) *Rhythm of entrance and/or porch projections.* On the East Jefferson Avenue buildings, the entrances and three-story porches are centered on each building; on the Fischer building, the entrance is also centered, but no porch exists.

(7) *Relationship of materials.* The dominant material of the district is brick, with cast stone as the most prominent secondary material. Wood is used for doors and window sashes, as well as porch structures. Concrete has replaced some cast stone with a corresponding loss of surface quality and decorative detail.

(8) *Relationship of textures.* The major textural effect is that of the low-relief surface created by the brick and mortar walls. The smooth surface of cast stone provides a major contrast, and also provides sculptural decoration. A third surface character is provided by the wood elements.

(9) *Relationship of colors.* The major color contrast is of the dark red brick contrasted with the gray cast stone. The brown woodwork provides color contrast without the dark-light contrast of the brick and cast stone colors.

(10) *Relationship of architectural details.* Detailing on the buildings derives from the Beaux-Arts tradition, although the buildings are not Beaux-Arts in style. Detail is concentrated at the parapets, on the porches, around the basement windows and around the second and third story windows of the outer bays. The use of a raised parapet with cast stone detail above the bay window bays, flanking the heavily detailed porches on the East Jefferson buildings, tends to strongly emphasize the central bay, which is brought forward toward the viewer by the porches. This emphasis is less strong on the Fischer building, which has no porches. Above the party wall of the East Jefferson buildings a cast stone panel bears the name "Chalfonte," while a similar panel above the entrance of the Fischer building bears the label "annex."

(11) *Relationship of roof shapes.* All three buildings have flat roofs hidden by parapet walls.

(12) *Walls of continuity.* The East Jefferson façades provide a wall of continuity a half block long; the side wall of one East Jefferson structure and the Fischer building also create a short wall of continuity along Fischer.

(13) *Relationship of significant landscape features and surface treatments.* Plantings are limited to the area in front of the East Jefferson buildings, where a wedge-shaped grass turf lawn raised above the level of the public sidewalk reaches from the sidewalk to the buildings. Mature foundation plantings of both evergreen and deciduous types line the foundation of the buildings. Straight concrete walks with steps at the public sidewalk provide access to the entrance porches. On Fischer, the buildings are at the sidewalk line. In the rear, there is paved parking and service area.

(14) *Relationship of open space to structures.* Open space in the front is landscaped lawn area, in the area parking and service functions are served by limited open space. There is a narrow open space between the apartments and the adjoining church to the west; only the public sidewalk and street provide open space to the east. Beyond the boundaries of the district, a major open space exists across East Jefferson Avenue in a public park, while to the north, a large paved parking lot provides a large adjacent open space enclosed by a concrete block wall.

(15) *Scale of façade and façade elements.* The façades are of moderate scale for multiple residential structures; large elements, such as bay windows and porches, are decorated with smaller scale elements largely of cast stone. Window and door openings are of moderate scale within the façades.

(16) *Directional expression of front elevation.* The joining of the two East Jefferson buildings at a party wall creates a façade wider than tall; this horizontality is countered by the arrangement of the façades in vertical elements such as porches and three-story bay windows. The coupling of second and third story windows by cast stone surrounds rising through both stories. The building on Fischer is more vertical in expression than those on East Jefferson Avenue simply because of the lack of another building adjacent at a party wall.

laws.title: Globe Tobacco Building Historic District
laws.content:
(a) An historic district to be known as the Globe Tobacco Building Historic District is hereby established in accordance with the provisions of this article.

(b) This historic district designation is hereby certified as being consistent with the Detroit Master Plan of Policies.

(c) The boundaries of the Globe Tobacco Building Historic District, as shown on the map on file in the Office of the City Clerk, are as follows:

On the south, the center line of East Fort Street; on the west, the center line of Brush Street; on the north, the center line of the alley running east-west between Brush and Beaubien; and on the east the westerly line of the easterly portion of Lot 19 of the Brush Farm Sub of Block 6 (L7/P224), said line being 11.61 feet west of the easterly line of Lot 19 at its southerly end, and 11.64 feet west of the easterly line of Lot 19 at its northerly end.
