(d) The elements of design, as defined in Section 21-2-2 of this Code, shall be as follows:

(1) *Height.* The Globe Tobacco Company Building is six stories tall on a basement.

(2) *Proportion of buildings’ front façade.* The front façade is taller than wide; the east and west elevations are wider than tall.

CD21:127
§ 21-2-144

DETROIT CITY CODE

(3) Proportion of openings within the façade. Areas of voids generally constitute 33 percent of the façade. All vertically rectangular openings are two times taller than wide, while round arched window openings are as tall as wide on the fifth story and taller than wide on the first story. The arched entrance opening is taller than wide. Basement window openings are square and slightly arched. The transom window over the secondary entrance at the northwest corner of the building is wider than tall.

(4) Rhythm of solids to voids in front façades. A rhythm of voids in solids is created by the regular placement of windows. The façade is articulated in five bays, each bay consisting of a pair of window openings per story from floors two through four between single-arched window openings on the first and fifth floors. A row of regularly spaced windows comprise the sixth story. There are a pair of basement windows per bay. The front entrance is centered on the front façade. The west elevation along Brush Street is similarly articulated with nine bays of similarly fenestrated openings and a tenth bay articulated differently due to the placement of a stairwell and secondary entrance at the northwest corner.

(5) Rhythm of spacing of buildings on street. Not applicable due to single-building district.

(6) Rhythm of entrance and/or porch projections. Not applicable due to single-building district.

(7) Relationship of materials. Brick is the major material of the building. Stone is used as a functional trim and detail. The entrance doors and window frames are wood.

(8) Relationship of textures. The main textural relationship is that of the low-relief pattern of mortar joints in brick contrasted with rock-faced or smooth stone trim. Brick voussoirs, raised brick detail in the form of denticulation and the corbel table, and recessed arches and raised brick pilasters contribute significantly to textural interest.

(9) Relationship of colors. The orange brick of the building is contrasted with light gray mortar and light gray stone. The front entrance is painted gray.

(10) Relationship of architectural details. Architectural detail is Richardsonian Romanesque in style and is mostly Architectonic in nature. Raised brickwork forms the denticulation, the arced corbel table, the pilaster capitals, and a row of paneled brickwork at the very top of the building. A projecting panel in the center of the front façade above the sixth story is surmounted by ball finials at its corners. Brick pilaster strips terminate in arches at the fifth-story level. Continuous stone sills and corner and impost blocks also create architectural interest.

(11) Relationships of roof shapes. The roof of the Globe Tobacco Company Building is not visible from the street.

(12) Walls of continuity. Not applicable due to single-building district.

(13) Relationship of significant landscape features and surface treatments. The building sits on its lot lines; therefore, no landscaping exists. A concrete public sidewalk exists between the building and East Fort Street on its south and Brush Street on its west. A concrete surfaced alley is to the north and a black-topped parking lot is to the east.

(14) Relationship of open space to structures. The building is sited on its lot lines on all four sides. To its south, west, and east are surface parking lots; to its north, across the alley, is the site of the former Wayne County Morgue Building.

(15) Scale of façade and façade elements. The Globe Tobacco Company Building is large in scale. Elements within the façade range from large, such as the pilaster strips resulting in arched openings, to small, such as the denticulation, with most elements in the moderate to large range of scale.

(16) Directional expression of front elevation. The front façade is vertical in directional expression, while its western elevation is horizontal in directional expression. This horizontality is diluted by the verticality of the individual bays.

(17) Rhythm of building setbacks. Not applicable due to single-building district.

(18) Relationship of lot coverage. The building occupies the entire lot.

(19) Degree of complexity within the façade. The front façade is straight forward in its arrangement of openings and its detail. Although the façade has

laws.title: Lee Burt House Historic District
laws.content:
(a) An historic district to be known as the Lee Burt House Historic District is hereby established in accordance with the provisions of this article.

(b) This historic district designation is hereby certified as being consistent with the Detroit Master Plan of Policies.

(c) The boundaries of the Lee Burt House Historic District, as shown on the map on file in the Office of the City Clerk, are as follows:

(1) On the north, the north line extended east and west of a parcel of land which is a portion of Lots 82 and 83 of the private plat of Lots 3-14 inclusive of Walker & Cooper’s Sub of P.C. 573, said parcel of land being described at L5507 P417 WCR.

(2) On the west, the center line of Concord Avenue.

(3) On the south, the south line extended east and west of that same parcel of land described in Subsection (c)(1) of this section and described at L5507 P417 WCR.

(4) On the east, the center line, extended southward, of the north-south alley lying between Concord and Canton Avenues. (The property included within these boundaries is a portion of Lots 82 and 83 of Walker & Cooper’s Sub of P.C. 573, as described at L5507 P417 WCR; the eastern half of Concord Street adjacent; and the western half of the alley adjacent to the eastern boundary of that same parcel.)

(d) The elements of design, as defined in Section 21-2-2 of this Code, shall be as follows:

(1) *Height.* The Lee Burt House is two stories tall.

(2) *Proportion of building’s front façade.* The front (south) façade of the Lee Burt House is wider than tall; the eastern addition to the original house makes it even wider. The eastern two-thirds of the front façade of the original house projects outward. The western elevation facing Concord Street appears slightly wider than it is tall.

(3) *Proportion of openings within the façade.* Window and door openings in the front façade, including those now blocked up with brick, amount to about 30 percent of the original area. Openings amount to about 20 percent of the west elevation. All window openings in the front façade and west elevation are two times taller than wide, not including the arched area. The exceptions are the basement windows, which are wider than tall. Although windows are paired in some locations, they are not so close as to constitute a single opening. Windows are one-over-one sash. The round arched upper part of the openings have been boarded up on many of the windows. Windows in the eastern addition and the rear, or north, elevation are also two times taller than wide, rectangular, and utilitarian in character. Attic story window openings in the rear (north) elevation are three times wider than tall and contain three panes each.

CD21:129
§ 21-2-145

DETROIT CITY CODE

(4) *Rhythm of solids to voids in front façade.* Voids are evenly spaced and regularly placed one on top of the other on the front (south) façade and west elevation, except where there is a chimney wall on the west elevation, resulting in a partially blank wall. On the front façade, the entrance opening is situated in the west-facing side of the projecting eastern two-thirds. The entrance vestibule, on the western one-third of the façade, encloses two elongated round-arched windows on the first story. Directly above, on the second story, are two similar windows. The first story of the eastern two-thirds of the façade contains two pairs of bricked in round-headed windows. Above the westernmost pair is a projecting five-sided bay containing three windows, and to its east is another pair of round-arched windows. The western elevation is composed of pairs of round-arched windows, except the lower southernmost window, which is a single round-arched window. Where rows or pairs of round-arched windows exist, an arcading effect is achieved. Windows in the eastern addition and the rear of the building are utilitarian in nature and, as a result, no regular rhythm of solids to voids is created, especially since many are bricked in.

(5) *Rhythm of spacing of buildings on streets.* Not applicable due to single-building district.

(6) *Rhythm of entrance and/or porch projections.* The projecting enclosed porch on the front (south) façade is flush with the projecting eastern two-thirds of the façade. A concrete block entrance vestibule was added to the rear (north) elevation near its northwest corner, and a wooden shed structure was attached near the northeast corner of the original house.

(7) *Relationship of materials.* The Lee Burt House is primarily brick; stone and wood elements are applied. Stone is used for sills, keystones, and impost blocks. Wooden elements consist of the front porch enclosure steps, five-sided bay and its supporting elements, cornice brackets, string molding, window frames and sashes. Some aluminum storm windows exist. The material of the roof is not visible from street level. The modern entrance vestibule added to the rear (north) elevation is concrete block and the shed addition on the rear elevation is wood.

(8) *Relationship of textures.* The major textural relationships are those of common brick and plain-cut mortar joints contrasted with the smooth surfaces of stone and wood. Carved keystones and impost blocks add considerably to textural interest, as does wood detail, such as the denticulation on the cornices of the porch and bay on the front (south) façade, the brackets fabricated from several pieces of wood, and the string molding. Brick detail in the form of raised brick voussoirs create a subtle textural relationship with the brick body of the house.

(9) *Relationship of color.* The major color relationship is between the orange brick, the natural light gray mortar, and the gray-painted wood and stone elements. Stone sills are natural light gray. Gutters are now painted brown. Unpainted aluminum storm windows cover some window openings. The concrete block addition to the rear elevation is painted green. The original colors of the house, as determined by professional analysis, are always acceptable.

(10) *Relationship of architectural detail.* Most of the detail is carried out in stone or wood and is located on the front (south) and west elevations. The stylized floral carvings on the keystones vary from first to second story on the front façade, and the impost blocks bear the same detail on both elevations. Where there are paired windows sharing a sill, a rhythm of arches occurs, due to the raised brick voussoirs around the round arches. The overhanging roof eaves are supported by large ornate brackets placed at regular intervals with smaller brackets between. Some of the large brackets are missing their pendants. A moulded wooden string course encircles the building at the foot of the large brackets. Stick-like brackets support the five-sided wooden bay on the front (north) façade. Its two outside faces not fenestrated contain wooden panels. Both the bay and the entrance vestibule have denticulated cornices. The perimeter of the wall of the front façade projects slightly, framing the area within. In general, the architectural detail is Italianate in style and restrained.

(11) *Relationship of roof shapes.* The shallow hip roof cannot be seen from the street.

(12) *Walls of continuity.* Not applicable due to single-building district.

laws.title: St. Charles Borromeo Roman Catholic Parish Historic District
laws.content:
(a) An historic district to be known as the St. Charles Borromeo Roman Catholic Parish Historic District is hereby established in accordance with the provisions of this article.

(b) This historic district designation is hereby certified as being consistent with the Detroit Master Plan of Policies.

(c) The boundaries of the St. Charles Borromeo Roman Catholic Parish Historic District, as shown on the map on file in the Office of the City Clerk, are as follows:

On the north, the center line of St. Paul Avenue; on the west, the center line of Townsend Avenue; on the south, east along a line 15 feet north of the south line of Lot 224 of Moses Field’s Sub (L8/P37) to its intersection with the alley running north-south between Baldwin and Townsend; thence north along the center line of said north-south alley to its intersection with the south line of Lot 237 of Moses Field’s Sub (L8/P37) extended west; thence east along said lot line to its intersection with the center line of Baldwin Avenue; and on the east, the center line of Baldwin Avenue. (These boundaries include north half of Lot 224 and Lots 225 through 237 (inclusive) of Moses W. Field’s Sub of P.C. 16 lying between East Lafayette Boulevard and Linden Park Avenue (L8/P37).)

(d) The elements of design, as defined in Section 21-2-2 of this Code, shall be as follows:

(1) *Height.* St. Charles Borromeo Roman Catholic Church is a tall single-story space that is approx-

CD21:131
$\S 21-2-146$

DETROIT CITY CODE

imately 60 feet to its eaves. The tower on the southeast corner of the building is also 60 feet tall, not including its roof. The bell tower on the northeast corner of the building is approximately 100 feet tall. The rectory is $2\frac{1}{2}$ stories tall and the school building is two stories tall on a very high basement.

(2) *Proportion of building’s front façade.* The façade of the church is wider than tall, but appears taller than wide due to its vertical elements, such as the corner towers. The secondary elevation of the church along St. Paul is wider than tall. The rectory is wider than tall to its eaves, as is the school building.

(3) *Proportion of openings within the façades.* Openings in the façade of the church amount to approximately 20 percent. All of its openings are taller than wide or round. The façade of the rectory contains approximately 35 to 40 percent openings. Its four main window openings are wider than tall but contain three double-hung sash windows each that are taller than wide. In the second-story central section of the rectory’s front façade, the two windows are slightly taller than wide. The entrance opening of the rectory is subdivided into the doorway and two sidelights, each taller than wide. The façade of the school building is comprised of about 40 to 45 percent openings; all are taller than wide.

(4) *Rhythm of solids to voids in front façades.* The front façade of the church is divided into three projecting sections: the central portico section, the southeast tower, and the northeast tower. Voids are arranged symmetrically in a regular fashion within each section. The main portico section consists of three arched entrance openings sharing piers, thus creating an arcade. Above is a large rose window composed of round fixed-pane stained glass windows. An oculus is centered in the gable. The first stages of the northeast and southeast towers are identical with two rows of paired round-arched windows sharing a pilaster. The second stage of the southeast tower has three ocular windows beneath its cornice. The northeast tower has two rows of narrow elongated windows comprising its second stage. Its third stage consists of two ocular windows beneath a pair of arched openings sharing a pilaster and sill. This top stage of the tower is open on all four sides. The windows in the tower sections are frequently subdivided into three sections. Recessed sections between the portico section and each tower contain two single round-arched windows, one above the other, and an aedicule above. The fenestration of the rectory also exhibits a regular rhythm of solids to voids. To each side of the central section on both stories is a large opening containing three double-hung sash windows, the central one being wider than those flanking it. The windows are further subdivided by mullions and muntins. The second-story central projecting area that extends into a dormer contains a small rectangular window and an arched window; each are subdivided within. The sidelights flanking the single-door entrance are subdivided into two columns of square panes of glass. There is a regular and symmetrical arrangement of openings in the façade of the school building. The entrances in the projecting pavilions are double-doored with segmentally arched transoms. Basement windows and front entrances are directly above ground level. Above the entrances are banks of subdivided windows, the lower grouping consisting of three double-hung sash windows and the upper grouping containing double-hung sash windows in a palladian arrangement with an arched transom. The windows in the sections flanking the entrance pavilions are of the double-hung sash variety. They are arranged singularly at the ends and paired in the middle of each section, creating a definite rhythm of solids to voids.

(5) *Rhythm of spacing of buildings on street.* Inapplicable due to single-complex district.

(6) *Rhythm of entrance and/or porch projections.* Inapplicable due to single-complex district.

(7) *Relationship of materials.* The major material of all three buildings is brick. It is primarily contrasted with stone foundations, steps, window sills, lintels, belt courses, and other decorative trims of stone. The central portico section of the church is Bedford stone. Square tiles fill the spandrels and pediment of the front façade and transept arms of the church. Its roof and the roof of the rectory are Mediterranean tile. The roof of the school building is not visible from the street. Window frames and doors of all buildings are wood. The towers and some pedi-

CD21:132

laws.title: History
laws.content:
§ 21-2-146

ments of the church are topped with brass crosses. The church also contains metal cornices and copper flashing.

(8) *Relationship of textures.* The tapestry brick and rusticated foundations comprised of smooth stone with margins contrast with the smooth stone surfaces of the water course, belt course, trim, lintels, sills, and central portico section of the church. Tile in pediments and spandrels creates textural interest. Where brick and stone projects or recedes from flat surfaces of the church, rectory and/or school, textural interest is created. Carved stone on all three buildings and tile roofs on the church and rectory contribute significantly to textural interest. Wooden elements are generally smooth in texture, but create textural patterns where there is repetition, such as the eave brackets and the division bars in windows of the rectory, and the second story of the entrance pavilions of the school. In general, each of the three buildings contain textural relationships within themselves and relate texturally with each other.

(9) *Relationship of color.* The beige stone contrasts with the red-brown brick of all three buildings. Doors on the façades of the church and rectory are natural brown; one set of doors on the façade of the school is natural brown and the other is painted red. Window frames of the church, rectory and school are painted beige to match the stone. Tile in the spandrels and pediment of the church is green; the tile roofs of the church and rectory are red. Most of the crosses on the church roof are green; the one on the northeast bell tower is gold. Porch columns of the rectory are an orange-red terra cotta color.

(10) *Relationship of architectural details.* Architectural detailing of the church is consistent with its early Renaissance-Romanesque style. The round arch and the circle are common themes throughout the building. The portico of the church is recessed within a monumental arch and contains an arcade of three entrances and a large rose window above. The large arch is supported by columns set upon plinths. Classical elements include stylized acanthus leaves in the keystones, egg and dart and bead and reel moldings around arches and capitals, the balustrade beneath the rose window, and the rosettes in the spandrels beneath each entrance arch. Flanking the stone entrance section are modern motifs in raised brick with stone panels bearing interwinded motifs. All window openings have pronounced lintels and sills. Belt courses divide the stages of the towers. Architectural detail on the rectory is located on the second story projecting section, the brick pylons at the ends of the first-story porch, and the column capitals of the porch, which is designed in a modernistic geometric mode. The school building is also geometric in its ornamental design, most of which is located along its attic or parapet wall in the form of arcading and around the entrances and at the crest of the entrance pavilions. A belt course separates the high basement from the first story and also serves as a continuous sill. A belt course runs above the second-story windows. Modern diamond-shapes inset in panels of diagonally placed brickwork divide the first floor of the school from the second.

(11) *Relationship of roof shapes.* St. Charles Church has intersecting pitched gable roofs forming the front of the building and the transept arms. Over the rear section of the church is a hip roof; minor gables and hips over ancillary spaces and side entrances add complexity to the overall roof configuration. The roof of the fleche over the crossing and the roofs over the towers are shallow hips. The rectory has a shallow hip roof with a flat top; its front dormer has a barrel-vaulted roof. The roof of the school is not visible from the street.

(12) *Walls of continuity.* Because of the similar setbacks of the church and rectory, a short wall of continuity is created along Baldwin.

(13) *Relationship of significant landscape features and surface treatments.* Small grass turf areas exist to the sides of the front steps of the church, between the transoms and tower projections on the north side, and to the west, or rear, of the church. On the south side of the church, between the church and the rectory, is an asphalt driveway and parking area that extends between the rectory and school as well. A chain-link fence encloses the rear yard and rear side yards of the church. The rectory and school building have shallow flat grass turf front yards. Foundation plantings are planted around the front porch of the rectory. The public sidewalks and

CD21:133
§ 21-2-146

DETROIT CITY CODE

walks leading to the front entrances of all three buildings are concrete. There are wood telephone and light poles in the area.

(14) Relationship of open space to structures. Open space to the sidewalk exists in the front, north side and rear of the church, the front of the rectory, and the front of the school building in the form of shallow grass turf areas. The asphalt parking lot exists within the complex of buildings, creating an enclosed space.

(15) Directional expression of front elevation. The directional expression of the church is vertical, due to the vertical thrust of major elements, such as the corner towers and pediment gable. The horizontal directional expression of the rectory is interrupted by the second-story central motif which extends vertically, forming a dormer. The directional expression of the school is horizontal.

(16) Scale of façade and façade elements. The scale of St. Charles Borromeo Church is monumental. Its tripartite portico and rose window within the arch and corner towers contribute greatly to its monumental appearance. Elements within, such as the windows, are outlined boldly, and are generally moderate in scale. The rectory is moderate in scale for a single-family residential building; elements within are moderate in scale while details are moderate to small. The school building is moderate in size; elements within range from large, such as the windows and entrance pavilions, to small, such as the carved stone and brick detail.

(17) Rhythm of building setbacks. The building line of the church, excluding the staircase, and the rectory, beginning at the porch line, are set back approximately similar distances from the public sidewalk. The school is set back a short distance from the public sidewalk on Townsend and is not consistent with the setback or the rear of the church to its north.

(18) Relationship of lot coverages. The church and school occupy most of their lots; the rectory has space on all three sides. The asphalt parking lot occupies most of the rear within the complex; it is enclosed by the buildings.

(19) Degree of complexity within the façades. The façade of the church is symmetrical, with the exception of the corner towers, which differ in height and appearance above their first stages. The arrangement of details and fenestration is not complex, although it is varied. The façades of the rectory and school are straightforward in massing and arrangement of fenestration and detail, but the details themselves are complex.

(20) Orientation, vistas, overviews. The church and rectory are oriented towards Baldwin; the school is oriented toward Townsend; for practical purposes, the rectory and church can be entered off the parking area. The church provides a landmark from all directions in the immediate neighborhood.

(21) Symmetric or asymmetric appearance. The front façade of the church is not symmetrical because the corner towers are different in height and appearance above the first stage. The rectory and school are symmetrical in appearance.

(22) General environmental character. St. Charles Borromeo Roman Catholic Church is a very visible special use element in an aging and declining residential area on the City’s near-east side. It stands as a physical reminder of the church as a focal point in the community.

(e) In accordance with Section 21-2-76 of this Code, the Historic District Commission is hereby authorized to consider interior features in certain portions of St. Charles Borromeo Church, located in the St. Charles Borromeo Roman Catholic Parish Historic District, and permits shall be required for such interior work in those portions of the St. Charles Borromeo Church as provided for in Section 21-2-71 of this Code as if such work were exterior work.

(1) The interior spaces of St. Charles Borromeo Roman Catholic Church, which are hereby made subject to the Historic District Commission’s consideration, are those spaces normally open to or seen by the public, including the nave, narthex, transepts, chancel, chapels, gallery, and side aisles. The altar in the crossing of the church, including the platform and carpeting it stands on, and the arrangement of the pews are not original. Areas not open to and not ordinarily seen by the public, including the sacristies, vesting rooms, basements, upper floors or attic areas, organ chambers, closets, service areas, and the entire interiors of the rectory and the school are not hereby subject to consideration. laws.title: History
Alexander Chapoton House Historic District
laws.content:
(a) An historic district to be known as the Alexander Chapoton House Historic District is hereby established in accordance with the provisions of this article.

(b) This historic district designation is hereby certified as being consistent with the Detroit Master Plan of Policies.

(c) The boundaries of the Alexander Chapoton House Historic District, as shown on the map on file in the Office of the City Clerk, are as follows:

The north 32 feet of the south 71.60 feet of Lot 74 of the plat of the Beaubien Farm as recorded in L6/P475, W.C.R.; the north and south boundaries being extended eastward, the eastern boundary is the center line of Beaubien. (These boundaries include the north 32 feet of the south 71.60 feet of Lot 74 of the plat of the Beaubien Farm as recorded in L6/P475, W.C.R.)

(d) The elements of design, as defined in Section 21-2-2 of this Code, shall be as follows:

(1) *Height.* The Chapoton House is three stories tall on a basement.

(2) *Proportion of building’s front façade.* The façade is taller than wide.

(3) *Proportion of openings within the façade.* Windows and the entrance opening amount to approximately 22 percent of the front façade area. The entrance and all window openings are taller than wide, with the exception of the basement windows, which are three times wider than tall. Windows on floors one through three are of the one-over-one double-hung sash variety while the basement windows each consist of three square panes placed horizontally. Windows in the north and rear elevations are of the six-over-six double-hung sash type.

(4) *Rhythm of solids to voids in front façade.* The front façade is divided vertically into three sections by the arrangement of windows. On the first story, the south and central sections con-

CD21:135
§ 21-2-147

DETROIT CITY CODE

tain one window opening each, with the recessed entrance comprising most of the north section. The upper two stories are composed of one window in the north and south sections and a pair of windows in the central section. Second-story windows are segmentally arched while third-story windows have round arches. Upper-story windows are not vertically aligned with the first-story fenestration.

(5) Rhythm of spacing of buildings on streets. Not applicable due to single-building district.

(6) Rhythm of entrance and/or porch projection. Not applicable due to single-building district.

(7) Relationship of materials. The major materials are brick and mortar. A tin cornice supported on wooden brackets tops the front façade, and the window frames and sashes are wood. Storm windows are aluminum. The water table, belt course, foundations, keystones, impost blocks, and sills are stone. Tin panels occupy the area above the first-story windows, and the openings on the first story have cloth awnings above them. The roof deck railing is metal, as is the modern stair railing at the entrance. The double doors and entry vestibule are oak.

(8) Relationship of textures. The major textural relationship is the rough surface created by the brick and recessed mortar joints contrasted with the smoother appearance of the stone, pressed tin, and wooden surfaces.

(9) Relationship of color. The major color impression is that of the orange brick and light gray mortar joints. Window sashes, window frames, and storm windows are black in color, as is the cornice. The stone is light gray and the tin panels are beige to look like stone. The double doors and the paneled entry vestibule are natural oak in color. Awnings above the first-story openings are beige with black trim.

(10) Relationship of architectural details. Raised brick frames the building, and the wooden cornice supported by five simple brackets tops it off. Paneled and glazed double doors are set into the paneled-entry porch. Decorative pressed tin panels are located above the segmentally arched first-story windows and below the belt course separating the first story from the second. Corner blocks incised with stylized floral motifs in the Eastlake style are at the upper corners of the

first story and the ends of the belt course are incised with a stylized floral motif. Brick hood molds broken with stone keystones incised with floral motifs rest on molded stone impost blocks. The simple window sills of the third story rest on small console blocks. The central pair of windows on the second and third stories share a pilaster and impost block, and on the third story they share a sill. Overall, the Chapoton House is composed of architectural detail from the 1870s and 1880s.

(11) Relationship of roof shapes. The flat roof cannot be seen from ground level. The railing of the recent rooftop addition can be seen from the street.

(12) Walls of continuity. Not applicable due to single-building district.

(13) Relationship of significant landscape features and surface treatments. The building is sited on the east and south lot lines. The front of the building abuts the concrete public sidewalk. Two trees are planted in sidewalk planters which are brick-paved. On the north of the building is a shallow side yard, enclosed by a wrought iron fence, and on the west is a shallow rear yard, enclosed by chain-link fence. Overall, there are no significant surface treatments to the rear and sides of the building.

(14) Relationship of open space to structure. No open space exists in this single-building district other than the small side yard on the north and the shallow rear yard on the west. The public sidewalk is directly in front of the building, and there are parking lots to the north, south, and west.

(15) Scale of façade and façade elements. The façade is small in scale for a downtown building. Elements within are also small in scale with the window and entrance openings creating the largest elements within the façade.

(16) Directional expression of front elevation. The directional expression is vertical.

(17) Rhythm of building setbacks. Not applicable due to single-building district.

(18) Relationship of lot coverages. The Chapoton House occupies 90 to 95 percent of its lot.

laws.title: Cass Avenue Methodist Episcopal Church Historic District
laws.content:
(a) An historic district to be known as the Cass Avenue Methodist Episcopal Church Historic District is hereby established in accordance with the provisions of this article.

(b) This historic district designation is hereby certified as being consistent with the Detroit Master Plan of Policies.

(c) The boundaries of the Cass Avenue Methodist Episcopal Church Historic District, as shown on the map on file in the Office of the City Clerk, are as follows:

Beginning at the point of intersection of the center lines of Cass Avenue and Selden Avenue, and proceeding northerly along the center line of Cass Avenue to its intersection with the north boundary (extended eastward and westward) of Lot 2 of the Milo A. Smith Subdivision; thence westerly along the north boundary of said Lot 2 as extended to its intersection with the center line of the alley running northerly and southerly between the easterly boundary of Lot 24 and the westerly boundary of Lots 1 and 2 of the aforementioned subdivision; thence southerly along the center line of said alley to its intersection with the center line of Selden Avenue; thence easterly along the center line of Selden Avenue to the point of beginning. (Legal Description: Lots 1 and 2, Milo A. Smith Subdivision, Block 94 of the Cass Farm, Liber 1, page 117.)

(d) The elements of design, as defined in Section 21-2-2 of this Code, shall be as follows:

(1) *Height.* The church itself is a tall single story, about 50 feet to the roof ridge, with a 76-foot tower at the corner; the adjoining office and chapel structure is two stories tall; the later addition at the north side is one story tall.

(2) *Proportion of building’s front façades.* The façades of the sanctuary are wider than tall, with low eaves in relationship to the roof height. The façade of the chapel building on Selden is taller than wide.

(3) *Proportion of openings within the façade.* All windows are taller than wide; some windows facing the alley are grouped into openings wider than tall. Door openings are all taller than wide. Openings range from nine percent (east façade of the sanctuary) to 15 percent (Selden façade taken as a whole) of the wall surface of the façades.

(4) *Rhythm of solids to voids in front façades.* On the three major façades of the sanctuary, a large window or group of large windows is centered in the upper wall, with smaller windows aligned at the interior eye level below. On the north and south, these small windows are grouped at right and left; in the east façade they are a single row in the wall of the narthex, which stands forward from the main wall of the sanctuary. Doors are at the corners of the façades. The façade of the chapel building has windows symmetrically arranged on first and second stories. The connecting façade between sanctuary and chapel on Selden has doors and windows asymmetrically arranged.

(5) *Rhythm of spacing of buildings on streets.* Inapplicable due to single-building complex district.

(6) *Rhythm of entrance and/or porch projections.* Inapplicable due to single-building district.

(7) *Relationship of materials.* The major material, used to face the Selden and Cass façades and the north façade of the church proper, is grafton stone trimmed with ionia sandstone. Common brick is used for the west side of the building,

CD21:137
§ 21-2-148

DETROIT CITY CODE

and buff brick for the addition at the northwest façade. Limestone forms the foundation of all 19th Century portions of the complex; wood is used for doors, windows, and trim. Roof surfaces are of asphalt shingle; one small conical roof is slated and the tower is covered in pressed metal in imitation of Spanish tile. Glass forms a major surface of the exterior; generally in large sheets covering leaded glass.

(8) Relationship of textures. The major texture is the rockfaced coursed ashlar stonework set in mortar joints; the major textural contrast is with the smooth sheets of glass in the windows of the façades. Limited wooden trim and doors provide smooth contrasting surfaces, and carved stonework provides textural points of emphasis. The formed sheet metal roof of the tower is richly textural, while the asphalt shingle of the main roof is lacking in textural interest. Brick laid in mortar is the major texture of the alley façade and the buff brick addition.

(9) Relationship of colors. The major color at the time of designation is the charcoal color of the soiled stone; small cleaned areas indicate a natural stone color of golden beige contrasted with accents of light pinkish stone. The tower roof is green in imitation of oxidized copper; the asphalt shingles are black, and the small area of slate is in variegated Vermont slate colors. The doors of the sanctuary are the golden-brown of finished wood, while other woodwork is painted dark green, or dark brown. Red and buff brick colors occur in the alley and at the northwest corner of the building, generally away from the most common public view of the buildings.

(10) Relationship of architectural details. Details on the building are Architectonic in character and in the vocabulary of the Romanesque Revival. Carved stone details, including the tympanums of the tower doors, arch-topped windows and the hardware of the doors, are immediately apparent details.

(11) Relationship of roof shapes. The complex combines gabled roofs on the main sanctuary with hipped roofs on the chapel structure, which also has an intersecting gabled roof. The roof of the tower is, in effect, a steep hip; the roof of the northwest addition is flat.

(12) Walls of continuity. Inapplicable due to single-building district.

(13) Relationship of significant landscape features and surface treatments. A narrow lawn exists between the sanctuary and the concrete sidewalks on the south and east façades; the grass turf is divided from the public right-of-way by a low chain-link fence. The western portion of the property along Selden is paved from the chapel building to the street. The west façade faces on a paved public alley; the open space to the north of the sanctuary is paved and separated from the Cass Avenue sidewalk by a tall chain-link fence.

(14) Relationship of open space to structure. There is a narrow strip of fenced lawn between the sanctuary and the sidewalks on Cass and Selden, and a narrow paved area between the chapel structure and the Selden sidewalk. There is also a paved open area north of the sanctuary and east of the northwest façade. The building appears to be immediately adjacent to the right-of-way of the alley to the west. Open space in the area adjacent to the district is vacant land created by building demolition in a formerly intensely developed urban setting.

(15) Scale of façades and façade elements. Although the sanctuary is not large, the scale of the façades is intended to create a massive appearance. The large expanses of rough stonework and the use of very large elements, such as the upper windows and the tower, and very small elements like the lower windows of the sanctuary and the tower windows, combine to create a massive character. The Selden façade of the chapel structure is both modestly scaled and has neither very large nor very small elements within it.

(16) Directional expression of front elevation. The directional expression of both the Cass and Selden façades is horizontal. The relatively low eaves and the arrangement of large upper windows over rows of small windows contribute to a structure that imparts feelings of weightiness and solidity, standing heavily upon the ground. On the Cass façade, the horizontal elements of the narthex wall standing forward of the sanctuary wall adds to the horizontal feeling; similarly, the single-story extension in front of the

laws.title: D.M. Ferry & Company Superintendent’s House Historic District
laws.content:
(a) An historic district to be known as the D.M. Ferry & Company Superintendent’s House Historic District is hereby established in accordance with the provisions of this article.

(b) The historic district designation is hereby certified as being consistent with the Detroit Master Plan of Policies.

(c) The boundaries of the D.M. Ferry & Company Superintendent’s House Historic District, as shown on the map on file in the Office of the City Clerk, are as follows:

On the east, the east lot line of Lot 4, Block 38 of Ferry and Lyster’s Subdivision of the A. Beaubien Farm (L12/P42); on the north, the center line of East Ferry Avenue; on the west, a line drawn 20 feet west of the west lot line of Lot 3, Block 38 of Ferry and Lyster’s Subdivision of the A. Beaubien Farm (L12/P42); on the south, the center line of the alley running east-west between St. Antoine and the Walter P. Chrysler Service Drive. (Legal description: east 20 feet of Lot 2 and all of Lots 3 and 4 of Block 38 of Ferry and Lyster’s Subdivision of the A. Beaubien Farm (L12/P42).)

(d) The elements of design, as defined in Section 21-2-2 of this Code, shall be as follows:

(1) *Height.* The superintendent’s house is $2\frac{1}{2}$ stories in height, meaning it is two full stories with an attic within the roof.

(2) *Proportion of building’s front façade.* The front façade is wider than tall, excluding the roof. It is articulated in receding and projecting wall sections. The side elevations are wider than tall.

(3) *Proportion of openings within the façade.* Window and door openings amount to 33 percent of the front façade area, excluding the roof. All window openings are two times taller than wide, with the exception of the fan window in the

CD21:139
§ 21-2-149

DETROIT CITY CODE

frontal gable. The entrance opening is taller than wide. A square skylight punctures the roof.

(4) *Rhythm of solids to voids in the front façade.* Each projecting or receding wall plane of the front façade is fenestrated within itself. The entrance section on the east side of the front façade contains a set of double doors. All window openings in the front façade are rectangular, with the exception of the segmentally arched squat opening between the entrance and the bay and the fan window in the gable. A boxy three-sided bay containing two elongated windows in its long, center face and one similar window in each of its side façades occupies the northwest corner of the front façade. All double-hung sashes contain one pane of glass per sash. While a regular rhythm of solids to voids may exist within sections of the front façade, irregular massing creates an overall impression of irregularity. Side elevations also display an irregular rhythm of solids to voids, containing segmentally arched openings on the first story, a window cutting through both the first and second stories, and on the west elevation, a three-sided bay window.

(5) *Rhythm of spacing of buildings on streets.* Not applicable due to single-building district.

(6) *Rhythm of entrance and/or porch projections.* The porch and six steps leading up to it on the eastern side of the front façade project outward. The side porch on the northwest corner of the house projects outward to meet the west elevation. No rhythm is created in a single-building district.

(7) *Relationship of materials.* The brick first story contrasts with the shingled second story and the limestone foundations. Sills and a small amount of trim are stone. Window frames, sashes, architectural detail, and porch elements are wood. Original roofing material has been replaced with asphalt shingles.

(8) *Relationship of textures.* The rough-faced coursed stone foundations and the shingled second story contrasts with the smoother brick of the first story. Wooden elements are usually smooth in texture, except when they are carved or placed in a repetitive fashion, creating textural interest.

Large panes of window glass create a smooth surface. Asphalt shingles of the roof generally do not contribute to textural interest.

(9) *Relationship of colors.* The orange brick of the first story contrasts with the beige stone foundations and brown painted shingles of the second story. Black trim is used throughout. The asphalt roof is black, as are the decorative security gates and the wrought iron fence at the front. The double doors are natural wood. The original colors of the house, as determined by professional analysis, are always acceptable.

(10) *Relationship of architectural details.* Architectural details are in the Eastlake decorative style and are concentrated on the porches, the gable, and a panel between the two windows above the entrance. Wood is elaborately carved and turned, reminiscent of furniture design. The second story is clad in octagonal shingles; wooden stylized brackets support the overhang of the shingles above the first story. There are stone impost blocks and the upper corners or the central first-floor window. Architectural detail, such as the overhang of the shingled second story, is carried around to the side elevations of the building. The brick chimney on the west elevation is clustered. The building at 612 E. Ferry is very rich in architectural detail.

(11) *Relationship of roof shapes.* The house has a multi-planed roof, its main roof being a steep hip. A gabled dormer intersects the main roof on the front slope and the main roof extends down through the second story to provide shelter for a shallow side porch on the west elevation.

(12) *Walls of continuity.* Not applicable due to single-building district.

(13) *Relationship of significant landscape features and surface treatments.* Foundation plantings of a deciduous and evergreen nature are located close to the front of the house. A brick wall curves around to the front steps from the public sidewalk. A straight-line front walk leading directly to the front steps from the public sidewalk is no longer functional. A six-foot-high decorative wrought iron fence is at the front, while the east and south sides are enclosed with stockade fence and the west side is enclosed with chain-link. laws.title: St. John C.M.E. Church Historic District
laws.content:
(a) An historic district to be known as the St. John C.M.E. Church Historic District is hereby established in accordance with the provisions of this article.

(b) This historic district designation is hereby certified as being consistent with the Detroit Master Plan of Policies.

(c) The boundaries of the St. John C.M.E. Church Historic District, as shown on the map on file in the Office of the City Clerk, are as follows:

On the south, the center line of Blaine Avenue; on the east, the center line of Woodward Avenue; on the north, the center line of Gladstone Avenue; and on the west, the center line of the north-south alley lying west of and parallel to Woodward Avenue. (Legal Description: Lots 99, 100, 101, and 102 of the McLaughlin Brothers Subdivision of Out Lot 4 and the southerly 150 feet of Out Lot 5 of the Subdivision of Quarter Section 45, 10,000 Acre Tract, L. 14, P.21.)

(d) The elements of design, as defined in Section 21-2-2 of this Code, shall be as follows:

(1) *Height.* The sanctuary is a tall single story on a high basement, about 72 feet tall to the roofline; the adjoining church house structure is two stories tall above the basement. The terrace row house building is also two stories tall. All structures have pitched roofs creating attic floors.

(2) *Proportion of buildings’ front façades.* The east facing façade of the sanctuary is taller than wide; the Blaine frontage is wider than tall, as is the church house to the north of the sanctuary. All façades of the townhouse building are wider than tall, especially facing Gladstone.

(3) *Proportion of openings within the façade.* All windows are taller than wide; many door openings contain pairs of doors, and are therefore approximately as wide as tall. Openings range from 15 percent to 30 percent of the wall surface of the various façades.

CD21:141
§ 21-2-150

DETROIT CITY CODE

(4) *Rhythm of solids to voids in front façades.* Voids are generally asymmetrical but vertically aligned in the various façades.

(5) *Rhythm of spacing of buildings on streets.* No rhythm is established by the church complex and the townhouses.

(6) *Rhythm of entrance and/or porch projections.* No rhythm is established by the church complex together with the townhouse complex.

(7) *Relationship of materials.* The dominant material used to face the church complex and the first floor of the townhouse is face brick. Face brick contrasts with stone trim and the slate of the sanctuary roof and the asphalt roofs of the church house and townhouses. Common brick occurs on the rear walls. Wood shingle and wood millwork are used extensively on the townhouses. Glass is a major element, particularly of the sanctuary portion of the church complex. Metal occurs in doors and in window frames in some openings in the church complex.

(8) *Relationship of textures.* The major texture is the extremely smooth and flat brick of the church set in mortar. The major textural contrast with the mortar-set brick on the church complex is with the smooth sheets of glass in the windows of the façades and with the smooth stone trim. On the townhouses, the texture of the brickwork on the first floor is emphatic and contrasts with the texture of wood shingling on the upper portions of the façade. Limited wooden trim and doors provide smooth contrasting surfaces. The slate of the sanctuary roof provides a low relief texture, while the asphalt shingle of the church house and townhouse roofs is lacking in textural interest. Brick laid in mortar is the major texture of the rear façades.

(9) *Relationship of colors.* The major color is the bright red of the "impervious" brick; this contrasts with the off-white of the trim stone and the grey asphalt shingles on the church house. The townhouses contrast dark red brown of the brick with the dark green painted shingling and the white painted millwork. At the rear is found the orange color of local common brick.

(10) *Relationship of architectural details.* Details on the church complex are architectonic in character and in the vocabulary of the Neo-Gothic and Tudor styles. Much of this detailing is extremely simple, especially on the sanctuary structure. On the townhouses, detail is largely carried out in wooden millwork derived from classical precedents and is domestic in character. Glazing bars, mullions, and muntins are the major details of the windows.

(11) *Relationship of roof shapes.* Gabled roofs are the major form in the district. The church complex has some flat roofs, particularly abutting the sanctuary. The 1902-1907 portion of the complex has a hip roof, but this is virtually invisible from the street.

(12) *Walls of continuity.* The church complex and townhouse complex do not form any significant walls of continuity.

(13) *Relationship of significant landscape features and surface treatments.* The "L"-shaped church complex is set well back on the site, creating a large lawn of grass turf facing Woodward Avenue, deeper at the center of the block in front of the church house wing. Grass turf lawns also exist between the sanctuary and Blaine, and in front of all townhouse units. Concrete sidewalks exist on Woodward Avenue, Blaine and Gladstone, and there are concrete walks leading to the various entrances. There is a paved alley at the rear. Some foundation plantings exist near both the church complex and townhouses.

(14) *Relationship of open space to structure.* The major open space is the large lawn of grass turf lying between the sanctuary and the townhouses and in front of the church house wing. Other narrower areas of grass turf exist between the buildings and the streets. The church complex is built at or very near the rear lot line adjoining the alley; the townhouses have a small rear yard space running behind them. The historic district exists in an area rich in churches and other institutions, and this portion of Woodward Avenue is notable for the repeated occurrence of large open spaces associated with institutional buildings.

(15) *Scale of façades and façade elements.* The sanctuary portion of the church complex has large expanses of façade with relatively small and simple façade elements, creating an impression of very large scale. The church house wing is more modest in scale and its façade elements more balanced so that an almost domestic scale

CD21:142

laws.title: History
laws.content:
§ 21-2-150

is suggested. The townhouses are domestic in scale and the façade elements are in accord; a domestic scale results.

(16) *Directional expression of front elevation.* The various façades are almost all horizontal in expression, except the Woodward Avenue façade of the sanctuary which is vertical due to the several vertical elements, including the pointed window.

(17) *Rhythm of building setbacks.* There is no rhythm of setbacks established.

(18) *Relationship of lot coverages.* Fifty-five percent of the area of the district is built upon, but most of the open space belongs properly to the church complex, while the townhouse building covers a high percentage of its site.

(19) *Degree of complexity within the façade.* The façades are not complex; particularly, the Woodward Avenue façade of the sanctuary is quite simple in its arrangement. The effect of the church complex lies in its materials and massing more than complex design. The townhouse façades are more complex with bays, entrance hoods, overhangs, and other details.

(20) *Orientation, vistas, overviews.* Situated on a corner, with an open space before it, the church forms one of a row of landmark structures on Woodward Avenue. The lack of doors in the Woodward Avenue façade of the sanctuary tends to give this element the feeling of being oriented to Blaine, although there is an entrance at the northeast corner. The church house orients to Woodward Avenue across the generous lawn space. The townhouse units orient to Woodward Avenue and to Gladstone.

(21) *Symmetric or asymmetric appearance.* The Woodward Avenue façade of the sanctuary is symmetrical; all other façades of the church complex are asymmetrical, as are the townhouse façades.

(22) *General environmental character.* The church complex forms a landmark quality structure on a major thoroughfare containing a number of such structures nearby. The townhouse units are a reminder of the mixed-use character of Woodward Avenue in the past. The district as a whole has and shares a highly urban character as part of the streetscape of a major thoroughfare.

(e) In accordance with Section 21-2-76 of this Code, the Historic District Commission is hereby authorized to consider interior features in certain portions of the St. John C.M.E. Church Complex, located in the St. John C.M.E. Church Historic District, and permits shall be required for such interior work in those portions of St. John C.M.E. Church as provided for in Section 21-1-71 of this Code, as if such work were exterior work:

(1) The interior spaces of the St. John C.M.E. Church Complex, which are hereby made subject to the Historic District Commission’s consideration, are those portions of the sanctuary normally seen by the public, including the nave, aisles, chancel, transepts, gallery, and eastern vestibules; and the chapel located in the front of the church house wing between the sanctuary and the Woodward Avenue entrance to the church house. These areas that are made subject to Historic District Commission consideration are shown on the floor plan on file in the Offices of the City Clerk, the Historic Designation Advisory Board, and the Historic District Commission. All areas, which are not mentioned in this subsection are excluded from Historic District Commission review, include offices and studies, sacristies, closets, rest rooms, basements, organ chambers, lounges, dining room and kitchen facilities, meeting rooms, hallways, staircases, and entrance vestibules other than those specified.

(2) In considering proposals for the alteration, demolition, removal, or addition to any or all of the architectural features and permanent furnishings within the designated interior areas of the St. John C.M.E. Church Complex, the Historic District Commission shall use the following criteria:

a. Subsections (d)(1) through (22) of this section as applicable;

b. The architectural or historic significance of the existing or proposed structure, feature, permanent furnishing, or fixture, and its relationship to the architectural and historical value of St. John C.M.E. Church Historic District;

CD21:143
$\S 21-2-150$

DETROIT CITY CODE

c. The purpose of the designated spaces within the St. John C.M.E. Church and the needs of its owners, provided, that such considerations shall not bind the Historic District Commission to permit any work solely on the basis of such considerations;

d. The provisions of Section 21-2-75 of this Code; and

e. Any other factor, including aesthetic, which the Historic District Commission deems to be pertinent.

(3) As a guide in considering proposals affecting the designated interior spaces of the St. John C.M.E. Church, the Historic District Commission shall make use of a set of slides, taken by the staff of the Historic Designation Advisory Board prior to the effective date of this section, which was April 27, 1988, and represents the state of those interior spaces as of the date of designation. Copies of this set of slides, together with a list describing each slide and a diagram showing the relationship of the slides to the designated interior spaces, are on file in the Offices of the City Clerk, the Historic Designation Advisory Board, the Historic District Commission, and the Burton Historical Collection of the Detroit Public Library.

laws.title: Oakman Boulevard Historic District
laws.content:
(a) An historic district to be known as the Oakman Boulevard Historic District is hereby established in accordance with the provisions of this article.

(b) This historic district designation is hereby certified as being consistent with the Detroit Master Plan of Policies.

(c) The boundaries of the Oakman Boulevard Historic District, as shown on the map on file in the Office of the City Clerk, are as follows:

Both sides of Oakman Boulevard from Linwood to Davison, excluding the Linwood Commercial Front-

CD21:147
§ 21-2-152

DETROIT CITY CODE

age, and both sides of Oakman Court from Linwood to Oakman Boulevard, excluding the Linwood Commercial Frontage. (Legal Description: Lots 143-158, 172-178, 206-229, and 241-263 of Robert Oakman’s Ford Highway and Linwood Sub (L.35/P.59); Lots 191-241 of Robert Oakman’s Ford Highway and Dexter Boulevard Sub (L.36/P.85); Lots 168-239 of Robert Oakman’s Livernois and Ford Highway Sub (L.36/P.2); and Lots 361-416 and 457-575 of Robert Oakman’s Turner and Ford Highway Sub (L.44/P.96).)

(d) The elements of design, as defined in Section 21-2-2 of this Code, shall be as follows:

(1) Height. Most of the houses in the district are $2\frac{1}{2}$ stories in heights, meaning they have two full stories with an attic or finished third floor within the roof. Some of the more modern houses are two stories tall with flat or shallow roofs. A few more recent houses scattered around the district are $1\frac{1}{2}$ stories tall. Original subdivision restrictions required that no house be less than two stories in height. Two four-story apartment buildings are located at the eastern end of the district. Garages are generally one to $1\frac{1}{2}$ stories tall. Detached garages are generally $1\frac{1}{2}$ stories tall. Additions to single-family residential structures shall be related in height to the existing structure; new buildings shall meet the following standards:

a. The eight adjoining houses on the same block face shall be used to determine an average height. The height of the two adjoining houses shall be added into the total twice, with a divisor of ten used to determine the average. Any new building must have a height of the main roof of at least 80 percent of the resulting average; in no case shall a new building be taller than the tallest roof height included in the computation. In determining the height of existing structures and proposed structures, the highest point of the main roof shall be used, even where towers, cupolas, or other minor elements may be taller.

b. The level of the eaves of a proposed new structure having as much or more significance for compatibility as the roof height, as average eave or cornice height shall be determined by the same process as that described in Subsection (d)(1)a of this section. The proposed new structure shall have a height at the eaves, or cornice, of not less than 90 percent of the average determined from existing structures, and in no case shall the eaves of cornice of the proposed structure be lower than the lowest eave or cornice height used in the computation, or higher than the highest.

(2) Proportion of buildings’ front façades. Proportion varies in the district, depending on style and age. Neo-Tudor style buildings tend to be wider than tall, excluding the roof, while styles derived from classical precedence tend to appear equal in height and width. Newer homes also tend to be square or wider than tall in proportion. No proposed building or addition shall create a front façade narrower or wider than those existing on the same block.

(3) Proportion of openings within the façade. Window openings are usually taller than wide; several windows are frequently grouped into combinations wider than tall. Window openings are always subdivided, the most common window type being double-hung sash, whose area is generally further subdivided by muntins. Casement windows on Neo-Tudor and Elizabethan houses are common, as are square bay openings subdivided into smaller panes. Leaded glass in windows, transoms, and sidelights are present in the styles derived from Elizabethan and Tudor precedents. Façades have approximately 15 percent to 30 percent of their area glazed.

(4) Rhythm of solids to voids in front façades. Where buildings are derived from English Medieval precedents, voids are generally irregularly and asymmetrically arranged. In buildings derived from classical precedents, voids are usually arranged in a symmetrical and evenly-spaced manner within the façade. Vernacular modern styles display a regular by asymmetrical rhythm of solids to voids.

(5) Rhythm of spacing of buildings on streets. In general, houses are situated nearer to one side of the lot line, providing space for a side driveway on the opposite side. Houses on the north side of Oakman Court and the north side of Oakman Boulevard are closer to the west lot line, as deed restrictions specified that houses on the

laws.title: Greater Shiloh Baptist Church Historic District
laws.content:
(a) An historic district to be known as the Greater Shiloh Baptist Church Historic District is hereby established in accordance with the provisions of this article.

(b) This historic district designation is hereby certified as being consistent with the Detroit Master Plan of Policies.

(c) The boundaries of the Greater Shiloh Baptist Church Historic District, as shown on the map on file in the Office of the City Clerk, are as follows:

On the south, the center line of vacated Benton Street; on the west, the west line, extended northerly and southerly, of Lot 296 of Crane and Wessons Sub of the T.A. Beaubien Farm north of Elizabeth (L1/P258); on the north, the center line of the vacated alley lying north of Lots 296 and 297 of the aforementioned Crane and Wessons Subdivision; on the east, the east line, extended northerly and southerly, of Lot 297 of the aforementioned Crane and Wessons Subdivision. (These boundaries include: Lot No. 297 of the Crane & Wessons Sub of T.A. Beaubien Farm north of Elizabeth (L1/P258).)

(d) The elements of design, as defined in Section 21-2-2 of this Code, shall be as follows:

(1) Height. The church building is a tall single-story space; its front façade is articulated as two stories on a high basement. The tower on the south-east corner of the original building rises slightly above the apex of the roof gable; it is articulated as three stories on a high basement, as seen on the east side elevation and the original blueprints.

(2) Proportion of building's front façade. The front façade is slightly wider than tall. Originally, the tower on the east end of the front façade and the front gable, as well as the vertical articulation of the west bay, emphasized the vertical; the proportions of the present front façade, with the front addition, is neutral in directional expression.

(3) Proportion of openings within the façade. Openings amount to approximately 20 percent of the front façade; the original façade had a similar percentage of openings. Although the openings that now exist roughly correspond to the original locations, their proportions and shapes are different. All openings on the original front façade, except the basement, had round arches and, when placed in groups, formed interesting arrangements; the openings on the front addition are rectangular and elongated, and read as individual windows. On the basement level of

CD21:151
§ 21-2-153

DETROIT CITY CODE

the original front was a rectangular door to either side of the stairs; these are absent on the front addition since the stairs are now on the interior, resulting in a top-heavy appearance. Ground level windows on the side elevations are square. The original portico with entrances facing frontally has been encased in the front addition; the entrances have been relocated to the addition’s side elevations, where there are modern glass and steel double doors with security gates.

(4) *Rhythm of solids to voids in front façades.* The front façade was originally divided vertically into three bays, the center one being the widest. It was divided horizontally into three sections also, these being the high basement, the portico level, and the upper story. The portico was approached by steep steps; to their sides were secondary entrances. In the present front addition, the ground level has no voids; it is solid wall. The central section of the middle level is composed of three tall rectangular windows; to each side in the outer bays is one tall rectangular window. The upper level contains three shorter rectangular windows in the middle bay and no other voids. In general, the fenestration and setting of panes of glass within the openings follow a regular arrangement.

(5) *Rhythm of spacing of building on street.* Inapplicable due to single-building district.

(6) *Rhythm of entrance and/or porch projections.* There are no entrances or porch projections on the front addition to the church. The building as it originally appeared had a multi-stepped portico that projected from the front façade; secondary entrances were flush with the wall at ground level. The present entrances are one step above ground level on the side elevations of the front addition.

(7) *Relationship of materials.* The primary materials are brick and mortar. Stone is utilized for coping, sills on the front addition, and rustication of the high basement as seen on the side elevations. Stone was more prominent in the original building, as more of the high basement could be seen, the portico was present, and the stairs projected outward. The roof is asphalt; the windows of the front addition contain four to seven panes of glass each. The importance of glass has been reduced due to the reduction in size of the window openings on the side elevations.

(8) *Relationship of textures.* The major textural relationship is that between textured brick and slightly recessed mortar joints. Stone coping and sills, and the rusticated basement level, still seen on the side elevations of the front part of the original building contrast with the brick. Patterned brickwork, especially the quilt-like pattern created by the repetitious juxtaposition of three vertically laid bricks with three horizontally laid bricks as in the gable and the knobby pattern of a brick laid with headers projecting as seen on the side elevation of the tower, create a significant amount of textural interest; the multi-paned windows also do so to a lesser degree. The asphalt roof generally does not contribute to textural interest.

(9) *Relationship of colors.* The brick of the front addition is reddish brown; the brick of the original building is orange-brown. Two courses of buff-colored brick form the foundations of the front addition. On the side elevations the original window openings are partially filled with orange- and black-colored brick. The body of the church is painted red and the roof is pinkish-gray. This contrasts with the light gray mortar and stone of the coping, sills, and rusticated base. Windows are composed of multi-paned glass in blue, yellow and red.

(10) *Relationship of architectural details.* The building as it now exists has very few architectural details, although it originally had a significant number centered primarily around the portico. In addition to the patterned brick detailing of the original building that can be seen above the front addition and on the side elevations, the front addition itself has very simple detail in the brickwork. Above and beneath the first- and second-story windows of the front addition is brick laid vertically, contrasting with the American Bond of the body of the addition. Ribbons of horizontally laid bricks stacked one above the other are located at the corners and sides of side windows in the front façade. A row of bricks laid vertically is laid beneath the coping of the front addition. The keystone of the sec-
