laws.title: St. Stanislaus Historic District
laws.content:
(a) An historic district to be known as the St. Stanislaus Historic District is hereby established in accordance with the provisions of this article.

(b) This historic district designation is hereby certified as being consistent with the Detroit Master Plan of Policies.

(c) The boundaries of the St. Stanislaus Historic District, as shown on the map on file in the Office of the City Clerk, are as follows:

Beginning at the intersection of the center line of Dubois Street and the center line of Medbury Avenue, and proceeding southerly along the center line of Dubois Street to its intersection with the center line of

CD21:153
§ 21-2-154

DETROIT CITY CODE

Hendrie Avenue; thence eastward along the center line of Hendrie to its intersection with the center line of the north-south alley lying west of Lot 30 of Hannan’s Sub of Lots 89 through 94 of the west half of P.C. 91 (Plats) (L8 P75); thence northerly along the center line of said alley to its intersection with the center line of the east-west alley lying parallel to and between Medbury and Hendrie Avenues; thence easterly along the center line of said alley to its intersection with the eastern boundary of Lot 4 of the Braun Subdivision (L11 P40), extended north and south; thence northerly along said lot boundary as extended to its intersection with the center line of Medbury Avenue; thence westerly along the center line of Medbury to the point of beginning.

(d) The elements of design, as defined in Section 21-2-2 of this Code, shall be as follows:

(1) *Height*. St. Stanislaus Church is a single-story space that is listed in the Sanborn Maps as being approximately 40 feet to its eaves; the ridge of the roof is higher. The Sanborn Maps indicate that the towers rise to approximately 90 feet. Both school buildings are three stories on a half-story-high basement; the rectory is $2\frac{1}{2}$ stories; the boiler house is $1\frac{1}{2}$ stories.

(2) *Proportion of building’s front façade*. The façade of the church is taller than wide due to its towers, but gives an impression of balance with its tall towers widely spaced on either side of the three-bay central façade. The side elevations are longer than they are tall to their eaves.

(3) *Proportion of openings within the façade*. Openings in the front façade of the church amount to approximately five percent. All of its openings are taller than wide. Openings occupy a higher percentage of façade area in the other buildings; openings are generally taller than wide; sometimes individual windows taller than wide are combined and divided by mullions to fill openings in the masonry wider than tall.

(4) *Rhythm of solids to voids in front façades*. All voids in front façades are symmetrically placed. The front façade of the church is divided into five elements: the central pedimented bay, the flanking bays topped with inverted consoles, and the towers. Each of these five elements contains voids centered; the central bay and arched window above the doors; the side entrance bays niches immediately above the doors;

and the bases of the towers have windows. The side walls of the nave are divided by brick pilasters into four bays each containing a centered tall round-arched window; voids in the west transept façade are symmetrical. Both school buildings and the rectory have voids placed symmetrically in a regularly spaced pattern within each front façade.

(5) *Rhythm of spacing of building on street*. Not applicable due to single-complex district.

(6) *Rhythm of entrance and/or porch projections*. Each of the three façades facing Medbury have entrances centered; the two schools each have a central entrance contained in a projecting segment of the façade; the center of the three church entrances is emphasized by the flanking columns which project from the wall, and all three are served by a broad flight of stairs projecting to the sidewalk. The rhythm created is not emphatic, as only three structures are involved, but does emphasize central entrances.

(7) *Relationship of materials*. The major material is brick. It is contrasted with masonry as used on the foundations, steps, window sills, lintels, and other decorative trim. Foundations are stone; decorative trim on the church is most often cast stone. Wood is used for window frames, doors, and some carved detail. The high school windows are steel. The roofs of the buildings are covered in slate. Copper is used on the upper stages of the church towers, cupolas, and the like.

(8) *Relationship of textures*. A variety of textural relationships exist, the major one being created by the juxtaposition of the low-relief pattern of brick in mortar with the relatively smooth surfaces of stone, cast stone, or terra cotta. The foundations of the building are coursed ashlar. The water tables are smooth faced. Other masonry elements are smooth. Carved stone, cast stone, and molded terra cotta detail provides significant textural interest, where present, as does the smooth surface of wood. The slate roofs contribute to textural interest, as do the muntins and glass of divided window sashes where they occur.

(9) *Relationship of colors*. The light gray stone, cast stone, or terra cotta contrasts with the yellow or dark red brick and the dark grey of the slate

CD21:154

laws.title: History
laws.content:
§ 21-2-154

roofs. Front doors are painted a medium brown; elements such as window frames are painted cream; the steel windows of the high school are brown. Green copper on towers and cupolas provides contrast with the cast stone and weathered slate.

(10) *Relationship of architectural details.* The complex is stylistically diverse, but all styles used include significant architectural details, generally on the street façades.

(11) *Relationship of roof shapes.* All buildings in the complex have sloped roofs. The church and the schools generally have gabled roofs; the rectory and the boiler house have hipped roofs with flat sections.

(12) *Walls of continuity.* A major wall of large scale is created by the two schools which stand almost on the sidewalk on Medbury. The church façade is somewhat recessed from that line. No wall of continuity is created along Dubois.

(13) *Relationship of significant landscape features and surface treatments.* Few landscape or surface treatments exist on Medbury and Dubois other than paving and narrow areas of grass turf in front of the schools and the rectory. Low bushes exist flanking the staircase of the Medbury entrance to the church, and a large tree stands between the church and the grade school. There are hedges as foundation plantings in front of the rectory. South of the rectory is an open garden space, enclosed by a handsome iron railing which runs in front of the rectory and the garden of the Dubois side and on the Hendrie side of the garden. Open space behind the buildings is mostly for parking and service functions.

(14) *Relationship of open space to structures.* Significant open space exists only behind the buildings and in the garden to the south of the rectory; the major buildings are generally close together and close to the sidewalk. Open land to the east of the high school is not included in this district; the surroundings were, and remain, mostly built up with small-scale residential structures.

(15) *Scale of façades and façade elements.* St. Stanislaus Church is monumental in scale, and major elements, such as the towers, inverted consoles, entrance stairs, transepts and apses, are also large in scale. Other buildings are less monumental, but still contain large façade elements and have façades large in scale for their functions.

(16) *Directional expression of front elevations.* The directional expression of the church is generally balanced, due to the broadness of the façade offsetting the verticality of the towers and the central bay. The two schools are vertical in expression, while the rectory is horizontal.

(17) *Rhythm of building setbacks.* Not applicable due to single-building complex district.

(18) *Relationship of lot coverages.* Not applicable due to single-building complex district.

(19) *Degree of complexity within the façades.* The façades of the buildings are somewhat complex in massing and variety of detailing.

(20) *Orientation, vistas, overviews.* The complex is most strongly oriented to Medbury, with a secondary orientation to Dubois. The complex was built and exists within a setting of smaller-scale residential structures and streets, but is now visible from the Ford Freeway rising above its surroundings.

(21) *Symmetric or asymmetric appearance.* The façade of the church is symmetrical, as are the street façades of the schools and rectory. The side view of the church is made asymmetrical by the towers, the transepts, and the apses and sacristies at the south; visible secondary elevations of the other buildings are all asymmetrical.

(22) *General environmental character.* The complex is a landmark especially when viewed from the nearby Ford Freeway. It is typical of a large religious complex which dominates its residential neighborhood. This is emphasized by the view from the freeway with the St. Stanislaus buildings rising up from amongst the smaller scale residential buildings around them.

(e) In accordance with Section 21-2-76 of this Code, the Historic District Commission is hereby authorized to consider interior features in certain portions of St. Stanislaus Church located in the St. Stanislaus Historic District and permits shall be required for such interior

CD21:155
$\S 21-2-154$

DETROIT CITY CODE

work in those portions of the St. Stanislaus Church as provided for in Section 21-2-71 of this Code as if such work were exterior work:

(1) The interior spaces of St. Stanislaus Church which are hereby made subject to the Historic District Commission's consideration are those spaces which would normally be open to or seen by the public in a functioning church, including the nave, narthex, vestibules, transepts, chancel, and gallery. Areas not open to and not ordinarily seen by the public, including the sacristies, vesting rooms, basements, upper floors of the tower, attic areas, closets, and service areas, are not hereby subject to consideration. Elements of the interior subject to Historic District Commission review include, but are not limited to, the walls, ceilings, floors and flooring materials, columns, original main altar, subsidiary altars, shrines, communion railing, organ façade, glazing, stations of the cross, lighting fixtures, doors, baptismal font, statues and statue bases, and any other old or original elements of significance to the historic and/or architectural character of the interior.

(2) Two elements of the designated interior spaces are not hereby made subject to Historic District Commission review and approval; they are:

a. The location and number of pews, provided, that some pews shall remain in the building as examples; and

b. The freestanding marble altar installed after 1967 in the center of the chancel which may be removed without permit, provided, that no other element may replace it in that location without a permit.

(3) In considering proposals for the alteration, demolition, partial demolition, removal, or addition to any or all of the architectural features and permanent furnishings within the designated areas of the interior of St. Stanislaus Church, the Historic District Commission shall use the following criteria:

a. Subsections (d)(1) through (22) of this section, as applicable;

b. The architectural or historic significance of the existing or proposed structure, feature, permanent furnishing or fixture, and its relationship to the architectural and historic value of the St. Stanislaus Historic District;

c. The purpose of the designated spaces within the St. Stanislaus Church and the needs of its owners, provided, that such considerations shall not bind the Historic District Commission to permit any work solely on the basis of such considerations;

d. The provisions of Section 21-2-75 of this Code; and

e. Any other factor, including aesthetic, which the Historic District Commission deems to be pertinent.

(4) As a guide in considering proposals affecting the designated interior spaces of St. Stanislaus Historic District, the Historic District Commission shall make use of such evidence as may be available documenting the state of the designated portions of the interior at the time of designation. Copies of such evidence and/or documentation which is in the possession of the City shall be on file in the Offices of the City Clerk, the Historic Designation Advisory Board, the Historic District Commission, and the Burton Historical Collection of the Detroit Public Library.

laws.title: Woodbridge Farm Historic District
laws.content:
(a) An historic district to be known as the Woodbridge Farm Historic District is hereby established in accordance with the provisions of this article.

(b) This historic district designation is hereby certified as being consistent with the Detroit Master Plan of Policies.

(c) The boundaries of the Woodbridge Farm Historic District, as shown on the map on file in the Office of the City Clerk, are as follows:

Beginning at a point, that point being the intersection of the center line of Brainard and the center line of Trumbull Avenue; thence easterly along the center line of Brainard to its intersection with the center line of the north-south alley between Trumbull and Lincoln; thence southerly along the center line of said alley to its intersection with the southerly boundary, extended east and west, of Lot 16, Hodges Bros. Sub. of OLs 98-99-102 and 103 of the Woodbridge Farm,

CD21:156
HISTORY

§ 21-2-155

(L1/P308); thence easterly along said lot line and extended to its intersection with the center line of Lincoln Avenue; thence northerly along the center line of Lincoln to its intersection with the center line of Brainard; thence easterly along the center line of Brainard to its intersection with the center line of Gibson; thence northerly along the center line of Gibson to its intersection with the center line of Calumet; thence westerly along the center line of Calumet to the north-south alley lying between Lincoln and Trumbull; thence northerly along the center line of said alley to its intersection with the north line, extended east and west, of Lot 130, Hodges Brothers Sub. of OLs 98-99-102 and 103 of the Woodbridge Farm (L1/P308); thence westerly along the northerly line of said Lot 130 as extended to its intersection with the center line of Trumbull; thence southerly along the center line of Trumbull to the point of beginning. (The property included within these boundaries consists of Lot 16 and S. 8' of vacated Brainard, Lots 33-130, Hodges Brothers Sub. of OLs 98-99-102 and 103, Woodbridge Farm (L1/P308).)

(d) The elements of design, as defined in Section 21-2-2 of this Code, shall be as follows:

(1) *Height*. The buildings in the district range from one to five stories tall; the majority are $2\frac{1}{2}$ stories tall, meaning they have two full stories with an attic or a finished third floor within the roof. Multi-unit apartment buildings range from two to five stories.

(2) *Proportion of buildings' front façades*. Proportion varies in the district, depending on style, size, and age of the buildings. Victorian single-family buildings and the larger apartment buildings are usually taller than wide to the eaves; duplexes and two and three-story multi-unit buildings are often wider than tall or as tall as wide. Elements above the eaves, such as turrets and gables, increase the appearance of height where they exist.

(3) *Proportion of openings within the façade*. Areas of voids generally constitute between 15 percent and 35 percent of the front façades, excluding the roof. Many buildings have window openings within the roof, in dormers, gables or towers, adding to the number of voids. Most window openings are taller than wide, although when grouped together might achieve a horizontal effect. Queen Anne and Romanesque-style build-

ings may have some square and/or arched openings. Transoms over windows and doors are wider than tall. Window openings in gables, turrets, and/or foundations are often square or arched. A great variety of sizes, shapes, and groupings of openings exist in the district.

(4) *Rhythm of solids to voids in front façades*. Most single- and two-family houses of the Late Victorian Era display a great freedom in placement of openings within the façades. Voids in Italianate dwellings are generally more regularly arranged than those in Queen Anne or Romanesque-style buildings. Apartment buildings show a regular arrangement of voids.

(5) *Rhythm of spacing of buildings on streets*. The spacing of buildings was generally determined by the setback from the side lot lines. Because of the number of buildings lost to demolition, the original rhythm has been disturbed. Consequently, the present spacing of buildings on the street does not establish any particular rhythm. There is an appearance of a more intact streetscape where there are rows of houses on some segments of Trumbull.

(6) *Rhythm of entrance and/or porch projections*. Steps and porches exist on all of the residential buildings in the district. The positions of porches contribute to the variety of design of the houses; front porches are frequently off to one side of the front façades of single-family houses and at both sides or in the centers of the front façades on duplexes. No consistent progression of front porches contributing to the streetscape exists because of the vacant land between houses due to building demolition. Rear porches and side porches exist on most of the houses throughout the district.

(7) *Relationship of materials*. The district exhibits a wide variety of building materials characteristic of Victorian architecture. Brick is prevalent; there are a few wood frame houses. Some Queen Ann-style houses have brick first stories and wooden, either shingled or clapboard, second stories. Some wooden houses have been covered with asphalt shingles. Stone foundations and trim, either limestone, red sandstone, or concrete, were frequently used in combination with brick. Wooden details and trim are prevalent. Original slate roofs exist, although asphalt shin-

CD21:157
§ 21-2-155

DETROIT CITY CODE

gle roofs have replaced many of the original roofs. Slate is also visible on some gables and towers. One house on Trumbull is stucco. There are a few houses in which the original wooden siding is covered with asphalt siding resembling brick; and the church on Willis east of Lincoln is clad in artificial clapboard-type siding.

(8) Relationship of textures. The most common textural relationship in the Victorian buildings is that of several materials juxtaposed within the same building to create a variety of rich textural effects. Brick with mortar joints is the most common textural effect, and often contrasts with the texture of other masonry and/or wood. Where wooden second stories exist over brick first stories, textural contrast is created. Wooden shingles and/or clapboard on wood frame houses on Lincoln create substantial textural interest, as does carved or repetitious wooden detail. Smooth or rough-faced stone foundations and detail provide substantial textural contrast. Varying patterns of imbricated shingles or slates, when used on the same buildings, create textural interest. Whereas slate and wood shingle on roofs and in gables create substantial textural interest, asphalt shingled roofs generally do not contribute to textural interest.

(9) Relationship of colors. Paint colors generally relate to style. Victorian buildings display freedom in the selection and placement of color; other buildings in the district generally do not. Orange-red brick frequently contrasting with light gray stone or red stone is the most common color relationship. Where brick buildings are painted, red is the most common color, although other colors, such as green and light gray, are also present. The one stucco building is painted red. Window trim and sash colors include brown, gray, pale yellow, green, red, and white and generally relate to style. The Venice apartments are yellow brick contrasted with light gray masonry and red window frames. The Kenwood Apartments has light brown brick on its front façade and common orange brick on other elevations. The most common roof colors are brown, dark gray, green, and black and these are generally in the natural slate or stained wood shingle color range. One green tile roof in deteriorating condition exists on Lincoln. Colors known to have been in use on buildings of similar type in the 19th Century and early 20th Century may be considered for suitability on similar buildings. Original color schemes for any given building may be determined by professional paint analysis and, when so determined, are always appropriate for that building.

(10) Relationship of architectural details. Architectural details generally relate to style. The majority of the buildings in the district are from the Victorian period and are of the Italianate, Second Empire, Queen Anne, and Richardsonian Romanesque styles. Porches, window hoods and trim, cornices, dormers, turrets and gables are frequently treated with stylistic details in stone, wood, or brick; Neo-Georgian, Arts and Crafts, and Prairie buildings display simpler detail, usually around the windows, cornice, or within panels; in general, buildings in the district are rich in architectural details.

(11) Relationship of roof shapes. A multiplicity of roof types exist, and frequently within the same building. The predominant forms of roof are the hipped, mansard and gabled varieties, frequently punctured with dormers, sometimes with intersecting gables and conical roofs over towers. Porch roofs are in keeping with the style of the house. Victorian buildings generally have roofs of greater complexity than those of later styles in the district. Some commercial buildings and apartment buildings have flat roofs not seen from the street.

(12) Walls of continuity. Primary walls of continuity are created by consistent setbacks of adjacent building façades. Where there are rows of intact buildings, primarily on stretches of Trumbull, a wall of continuity exists; where there have been many buildings removed, primarily on Lincoln, the original wall of continuity is destroyed. The regular placement of O.P. lighting poles on Trumbull creates a secondary wall of continuity; this does not exist on Lincoln.

(13) Relationship of significant landscape features and surface treatments. The Lincoln streetscape consists of a 70-foot right-of-way with the widths of tree lawns varying by block, although most are narrow. The Trumbull right-of-way is 80 feet; tree lawns are also narrow. The Gibson right-of-way is mostly 40 feet wide and serves primarily as an alley to the houses on the east side of

(2) Proportion of buildings’ front façades. The apartment building is taller than wide; its secondary elevation along Beaubien is wider than tall. The other three houses are slightly wider than tall to their eaves.

(4) Rhythm of solids to voids in front façades. Neo-Georgian and Prairie-Style buildings exhibit a great regularity in rhythm of solids to voids.

(5) Rhythm of spacing of buildings on streets. The spacing of buildings is generally determined by the setback from the side lot lines. The buildings on East Kirby are very close together with little or no side yard space.

(d) The elements of design, as defined in Section 21-2-2 of this Code, shall be as follows:

(1) Height. Commercial and institutional buildings range from one-story to four stories in height; some have single stories with very high ceilings and balconies, such as Aijalon Church, the former bank building at 4138 West Vernor and Bowen Library. Buildings in Clark Park are generally one or one and one-half stories tall, with additional height in a steep roof. Residential buildings range from one and one-half stories to five stories, the smallest being the workers cottages seen primarily on Bagley and the tallest being the five-story Whitedel Apartment Building on Porter and Hubbard. The majority of residential buildings are either two or two and one-half stories tall, meaning they have two full stories with an attic or finished third floor within the roof. Where height specifications were included in the original subdivision restrictions, they should be complied with for new construction. Detached garages are generally one to one-and-one-half stories tall. Additions to residential structures shall be related in height to the existing structure; new buildings shall meet the following standards:

a. The eight adjoining structures on the same block face shall be used to determine an average height. The height of the two adjoining houses shall be added into the total twice with a divisor of ten used to determine the average. Any new building must have a height of the main roof of at least 80 percent of the resulting average; in no case shall a new building be taller than the tallest roof height included in the com-

laws.title: Art Center Music School Historic District
laws.content:
(a) An historic district to be known as the Art Center Music School Historic District is hereby established in accordance with the provisions of this article.

(b) This historic district designation is hereby certified as being consistent with the Detroit Master Plan of Policies.

(c) The boundaries of the Art Center Music School Historic District, as shown on the map on file in the Office of the City Clerk, are as follows:

On the north, the center line of Alexandrine; on the east, the center line of Cass; on the south, the lot line between Lot 7 and Lot 6 of block 93 of Sub of Part of Cass Farm, L.1, P. 75 (also P. 176-7) Plats; on the west, the center line of the north-south alley between Alexandrine and Selden. (Legal Description: Lots 7 and 8, Block 93, of the Subdivision of Part of Cass Farm, Liber 1 Page 175, also pages 176-7 Plats.)

(d) The elements of design, as defined in Section 21-2-2 of this Code, shall be as follows:

(1) *Height.* The building at the southwest corner of Cass and Alexandrine, hereafter referred to as the "Brown House," is $2\frac{1}{2}$ stories tall, meaning it has two full stories and an attic or finished third floor within the roof. A two-story garage was added between the Brown House and the one-story garage at the alley. The building to its south, hereafter referred to as the "Chapel Building," is two stories tall.

(2) *Proportion of buildings' front façades.* The front façade of the Brown House is approximately as wide as tall to the eaves, excluding the one-story northern projection to the north that contains the secondary entrance on the Alexandrine elevation. The Alexandrine elevation, including garages, is substantially longer than tall. The front façade of the Chapel Building is slightly wider than tall.

(3) *Proportion of openings within the façades.* Window and door openings amount to approximately 35 percent of the front façade area of the Brown House, excepting the roof, and about 25 percent of the front façade of the Chapel Building. A variety of proportions of openings within the façade of the Brown House exist; rectangular windows are either taller than wide, wider

CD21:170
HISTORY

§ 21-2-159

than tall, or square. The three arched openings in the Chapel are substantially taller than wide; the window openings above are slightly taller than wide.

(4) *Rhythm of solids to voids in front façades.* The double-doored entrance with transom of the Brown House is flanked by a two-story bay with a window in each face to the north and a single double-hung sash window to the south. Above the entrance at second-story level is a wide-bowed window with small panes. The octagonal tower on the southeast corner of the Brown House has multi-paned elongated windows in its first two stories; although its first story has been altered to allow for an internal transition to the Chapel; the top stage of the tower has columns between openings. At attic level in the frontal gable is a palladian window containing four double-hung sash windows flanked by fan windows. A small palladian window with arched openings is situated in the upper rectangular shingled section. Around the corner on the Alexandrine elevation in the one-story entrance section are large window openings and aluminum double doors. A variety of window openings on the Alexandrine elevation exists, including rectangular, square, and bowed. A five-sided sun room contains seven windows with transoms. The first floor of the Chapel Building is occupied by a tripartite arcade created by the arched entrance and flanking arched openings. Three identical multi-pane casement windows at the second story level are evenly spaced and centered above the arched windows.

(5) *Rhythm of spacing of buildings on street.* The Brown House and the Chapel Building are attached, forming a single complex. No rhythm of space is created.

(6) *Rhythm of entrance and/or porch projections.* The porch on the Brown House projects from the body of the house, but no steps to it now exist. Since the house is set back considerably from the Chapel Building and cannot be accessed by its entrance on Cass, no rhythm is created. The Chapel Building entrance recedes only slightly from the face of the building; it is accessed up two steps off the public sidewalk.

(7) *Relationship of materials.* The major relationship of materials on the Brown House is that of brick contrasted with sandstone trim and detailing. Slate shingles fill the gable. Wood is used for window trim, sash and some major elements, as seen on the tower and north elevation sun porch. The roof of the Brown House is now covered with asphalt shingles. The façade of the Chapel Building is all stone, with bronze doors and metal lanterns. The stone surface and detail turn the north and south corners and continue for a short distance until replaced by brick as seen on the south and rear elevations. The glass in the doors and windows is subdivided by metal glazing bars or decorative bronze.

(8) *Relationship of textures.* The major textural relationship on the Brown House is that of brick with recessed mortar joints, now somewhat obscured by paint, contrasted with rough-faced stone detailing and trim. Patterns of stone, such as the railings above the porches and incised spiraling of the columns, create major textural interest, as does stone when carved on the column capitals and corners of the lintels over the first-floor bay window. The texture of the stone Chapel Building is uniformly smooth but matted, contrasting with the sheen of the glass in windows and doors. The subdivided casement windows add texture contrast, as does detail in stone and bronze. Asphalt roof shingles generally do not contribute to textural interest.

(9) *Relationship of colors.* The Brown House is now painted light gray, but was originally orange common brick with red sandstone trim, details, and foundations. The shingled gable is also now the light gray. Wooden window frames and sash are painted a darker gray, and the replacement roof is light gray. The stone of the Chapel Building is natural beige in color; window frames are medium gray. The bronze doors and ornamental elements are greenish bronze in color; the metal lanterns are a gold-green.

(10) *Relationship of architectural details.* Details of the Brown House are characteristic of the Queen Anne style, and are carried out in stone and brick. The octagonal tower is the major architectural element on the southeast corner of the house. The porch is supported by stubby stone columns incised with spiraling lines. Its Corinthian capitals support the coffered porch ceiling, brownstone frieze, and second-story stone railing. The corners of the stone lintel over the

CD21:171
§ 21-2-159

DETROIT CITY CODE

bay window to the north of the entrance is carved in a Sullivanesque manner. The hexagonal slate-shingled gable with overhanging eaves contains a palladian window flanked by fan windows with keystones, and a small palladian window in the upper rectangular slate shingled section. There is a beaded molding running between the second-story windows and eaves. Continuing around to the Alexandrine elevation, a transverse gable projects outward over a shallow three-sided two-story section. The secondary entrance has the same decorative brownstone railing as the front porch, but is supported on brownstone pilasters with Corinthian columns. To the west of the transverse section towards the rear of the house is a large wood-framed sunroom with a bowed window at the second-story level. Some detail on the Alexandrine elevation in the form of circles and panels with squares within are carried out in brick. Architectural detail of the Chapel Building is carried out in stone or bronze and is generally cast or applied. It is carried out in the Egyptian Revival style popular for funerary architecture. The pair of decorative bronze doors exhibit bundles of stalks tied together; bronze lamps with a projecting stem and leafy motif flank the entrance. Centered above the spandrels between the three arched openings and the edges of the building are four rondels with ancient male profiles and inscriptions. Wreaths set in recessed squares are cast in stone above the second-story windows. The stepped-up parapet wall is a stylized representation of a gorge and roll cornice, with swags and draped motifs beneath the zig-zagged cornice continuing around to the north and south elevations of the building.

(11) Relationship of roof shapes. The Brown House exhibits a multiplicity of roof shapes characteristic of the Queen Anne style. The main roof over the house is a front facing gable roof with a steep slope on the Alexandrine side. This terminates in the large gable of the front façade at attic level. A lower hip roof extends from the southern slope of the gable, abutting the octagonal roof of the tower at the southeast corner of the building. Along the Alexandrine, or north, elevation, the slope of the roof is interrupted by a pair of gabled dormers and an intersecting gable. Further west beneath a hip roof with a singular gabled dormer is the first-floor sunroom with a flat roof. Further west, the attached two-story garage addition has a pitched roof; to its rear on the alley, the one-story garage has a flat roof. The roof of the Chapel Building is not visible from the street.

(12) Walls of continuity. Because the Brown House is set back and the Chapel is near the building line, no wall of continuity is created.

(13) Relationship of significant landscape features and surface treatments. The Brown House has a shallow grass turf area on the Cass and Alexandrine elevations. Foundation plantings exist, as well as hedges at the corner of Cass and Alexandrine. A black metal sign bearing the name of the school sits on the lawn near the corner. The rear of the property on the Alexandrine side near the garages is paved with concrete. The Chapel Building has no front lawn, but foundation plantings are located to the sides of the front stairs in the shallow setback area, serving as a unifying element with the Brown House. The public sidewalk is concrete; the alley is black asphalt. A concrete driveway runs along the south elevation of the Chapel Building.

(14) Relationship of open space to structure. There is a shallow grass turf front lawn to the Brown House along Cass and side lawn area along Alexandrine; where the garage entrance exists, the grass ends and concrete begins. Vacant space in the form of the driveway exists between the Chapel Building and the building to the south.

(15) Scale of façades and façade elements. The Brown House, built originally as a single-family residential structure, is moderately scaled with fairly large scale architectural elements, such as the tower, gable, and porch, attached. Details are proportionately moderate or small in scale. The Chapel Building is a relatively small scaled commercial building with small scale detail within. The large-scaled arched openings on the first story provide a sense of grandeur.

(16) Directional expression of front elevations. The division of the façade of the Brown House into three vertical sections, with the gable over the central and northern sections, and the vertical tower element in the southeast corner, provide vertical expression. However, large square window openings with transoms, long bowed window arrangements, stone railings, and the one-

laws.title: Zion Lutheran Church Historic District
laws.content:
(a) An historic district to be known as the Zion Lutheran Church Historic District is hereby established in accordance with the provisions of this article.

(b) This historic district designation is hereby certified as being consistent with the Detroit Master Plan of Policies.

(c) The boundaries of the Zion Lutheran Church Historic District, as shown on the map on file in the Office of the City Clerk, are as follows:

On the east, the center line of Military; the south, a line drawn 30 feet south of and parallel to the north line of Lots 80, 81, and 82 of the Stephen Livernois Estate, (Liber 180, Page 343); on the west, the center line of alley running north-south between Michigan and Buchanan; on the north, the boundary line begins on the center line of Military Avenue and passes through a point on the easterly boundary of Lot 15, said point being 13.17 feet northerly of and southerly boundary of Lot 15, and runs thence to a point on the westerly boundary of the easterly 49 feet of Lot 15, said point being 13.28 feet northerly of the southerly boundary of Lot 15; thence southerly 7.21 feet to a point on the easterly boundary of the westerly 101 feet of Lot 15, that point being 6.07 feet northerly of the southerly boundary of Lot 15; thence westerly to a point on the westerly boundary of Lot 15, said point being 6.31 feet northerly of the southerly boundary of Lot 15; thence extended in a straight line to the intersection with the center line of the alley running northerly and southerly between Michigan and Buchanan. (These boundaries include all of Lots 16, 17 and 18, and that part of Lot 15 being the southerly 13.17 feet on the easterly line of said Lot, and the southerly 13.28 feet on the westerly line of the easterly 49 feet, also the southerly 6.31 feet as measured on the westerly line of said Lot 15, and the southerly 6.07 feet as measured on the easterly line of the westerly 101 feet of Lot 15, all of the "Plat of Lillibridge and Latham’s Subdivision of Lots 85 and 88 of the Subdivision of the Estate of Stephen Livernois of Private Claim 574 (Liber 6, Page 55) and the northerly 30 feet of Lots 80, 81 and the northerly 30 feet of the easterly 22 feet of Lot 82 of the Stephen Livernois Estate, (Liber 180, Page 343—345 of Deeds, Wayne County Records).")

(d) The elements of design, as defined in Section 21-2-2 of this Code, shall be as follows:

(1) *Height.* Zion Lutheran Church is a single-story space that is approximately 22 feet in height to the eaves of the side elevations. The tower at the northeast corner of the church rises 65 feet. The parsonage is $2\frac{1}{2}$ stories tall, meaning that it has two full stories and an attic space.

(2) *Proportion of buildings’ front façade.* The façade of the church is wider than tall, as are the side elevations. The front façade of the parsonage is slightly wider than tall to its eaves.

(3) *Proportion of openings within the façades.* Openings in the façade of the church amount to approximately 15 to 20 percent. The double-door entrances in the front façade are approximately as tall as wide; the slender windows to the side of the main entrance and above the tower entrance are taller than wide. The large arched tracery window above the main entrance is taller than wide. The façade of the parsonage contains approximately 35 percent openings. Each double-hung sash window opening is twice as tall as it is wide. But where they are grouped together in pairs, the openings are square. The single entrance opening is flanked by narrow sidelights.

(4) *Rhythm of solids to voids in front façades.* The front façade of the church is divided into two sections—the main gabled section and the projecting tower section at the northeast end. The

CD21:175
§ 21-2-161

DETROIT CITY CODE

few voids are arranged symmetrically in a regular fashion within each section. Above the main entrance and tower entrance openings are blind traceried arches. The large stained-glass arched window in the gable is positioned above the entrance opening. Small elongated windows flank the entrance. Large, paired louvered arched openings are in the upper stage of the tower. Although not symmetrical, the openings in the front façade of the parsonage are also regularly arranged. The front, south, and rear roof slopes have a single dormer containing a pair of windows.

(5) Rhythm of spacing of buildings on street. Not applicable due to single-complex district.

(6) Rhythm of entrance and/or porch projections. Along Military, the two entrance projections of the church and porch projection of the parsonage are fairly consistent, due to uniformity in the front building line, although the entrance of the tower section of the church projects slightly forward of the main entrance.

(7) Relationship of materials. Limestone is the major material of the church. The roof is slate, and its flashing is copper. The front doors are wood, and windows contain stained glass. Wrought iron railings lead up the steps to the church entrances. The major material of the parsonage is pressed brick, with common brick at the sides and rear elevations; its window frames, bays, and dormers are wood. Window sills are masonry. The roof is clad in asphalt shingles. The steps leading to the porch are concrete; the porch railings are wrought iron. Storm windows of the parsonage are unpainted aluminum.

(8) Relationship of textures. The major textural relationship of the church is that of the smooth cut blocks of random ashlar with visible joints. The slate roof contributes significantly to textural interest. Secondary textural relationships exist, such as the juxtaposition of stone tracery with smooth stained glass and carved stone with smooth stone. The major textural relationship of the parsonage is that of textured brick with slightly recessed mortar joints juxtaposed with wooden elements and stone sills. The asphalt shingles on the roof do not generally contribute to textural interest.

(9) Relationship of color. The beige stone of the church contrasts with the brown/orange brick of the parsonage. The roof of the church is composed of natural color slate, gray being the most predominant color. Copper flashing is green. The natural wood doors of the church contrast with the stone color of the church. The brown/orange brick of the front façade of the parsonage contrasts with the orange common brick of its three other elevations and its beige masonry sills. It has black roof shingles and black porch railings. Wooden elements, such as the bays, window frames, and dormers, are painted gray.

(10) Relationship of architectural details. The architectural elements and details of Zion Lutheran Church reflect its Neo-Gothic style. Buttresses exist to the sides of the entrance, the corners of the front façade, at the transition between the main face of the front façade and the projecting tower section, and on the side elevations at corners and between aisle windows. The crenelated tower on the northeast corner terminates with a louvered belfry. Above the molded and carved central doorway in the gable of the main section of the church façade is a large traceried window; at the apex of the large gable is a stone cross. The entrance doors are composed of square panels, some of which are glass forming a cross, the others are wood. Pointed arched openings contain molded stone mullions and tracery. The parsonage is of vernacular Prairie style with little detail; its front façade features a shallow bay on the first floor.

(11) Relationship of roof shapes. The main roof of the church is a front-facing gable with a transverse gable over the crossing and transepts. The roof of the crenelated tower is not visible. The hip roof of the parsonage has a projecting hip roof dormer on three of its faces.

(12) Walls of continuity. The two buildings comprising this district contribute to the wall of continuity created by the existing residential buildings on the street outside the district.

(13) Relationship of significant landscape features and surface treatments. The church is landscaped with foundation plantings at its southeast corner and ivy on the walls between the main body and the tower section. Both the parsonage and

CD21:176

laws.title: History
laws.content:
§ 21-2-161

church building have shallow grass turf front yards. A low buff brick wall extends from the northeast corner of the church eastward and northward to form a courtyard to the north. On the tower section to the south of the entrance is a State of Michigan Historical Marker; the church sign is on the lawn. Planted along the front line of the parsonage is a hedge of privet. There are foundation plantings to the sides of the porch steps. A driveway runs along the south side of the parsonage.

(14) *Relationship of open space to structures.* A three-sided courtyard is created between the church and the school; the open end is separated from the street by a low masonry wall and gated entrance. There is space between the church and the parsonage in the form of a side yard, and the parsonage has a rear yard. A church parking lot and private residences are located across from the church on Military Avenue.

(15) *Directional expression of front elevation.* The directional expression of the church is vertical, due to the vertical thrust of major elements, such as the corner tower and frontal gable roof. The directional expression of the parsonage is neutral.

(16) *Scale of façade and façade elements.* Zion Lutheran Church rises above the residential structures and school on the street; its scale in that context is grand, although it is of moderate size for its building type. Elements comprising the front façade, such as the tower, the gable, and its tracery window, are large in scale. The parsonage is a moderate scale residential structure with no exterior detail.

(17) *Rhythm of building setbacks.* The church and the parsonage are set back approximately the same distance from the public sidewalk.

(18) *Relationship of lot coverages.* The church and parsonage occupy approximately 50 percent of the parcel. Both have shallow front lawn areas; the parsonage has a rear yard while the church building occupies most of its lot.

(19) *Degree of complexity within the façades.* The façade of the church and the parsonage are straightforward in their arrangements of elements and articulation of details; each has a low degree of complexity.

(20) *Orientation, vistas, overviews.* The church and rectory are oriented towards Military, a residential street. The church school is connected to the north elevation of the church at its western end.

(21) *Symmetric or asymmetric appearance.* The church is asymmetrical in appearance due to the tower on the northeast corner; it is otherwise symmetrical. The parsonage is asymmetrical but results in a balanced composition.

(22) *General environmental character.* The church and parsonage are located on a residential side street in the first block off of Michigan Avenue, a busy commercial thoroughfare. Due to the existence of small-to-moderate scale residential buildings, vacant lots on Military and behind the district on Livernois and the industrial nature of land to the east, the overall character is of an aging, mixed-use urban area. Zion Lutheran Church and other substantial church buildings in the immediate vicinity stand as physical reminders of religious institutions as focal points of a once thriving community.

(e) In accordance with Section 21-2-76 of this Code, the Historic District Commission is hereby authorized to consider interior features in certain portions of Zion Lutheran Church, located in the Zion Lutheran Church Historic District, and permits shall be required for such interior work in those portions of the Zion Lutheran Church as provided for in Section 21-2-71 of this Code as if such work were exterior work.

(1) The interior spaces of Zion Lutheran Church which are hereby made subject to the Historic District Commission’s consideration are those spaces normally open to or seen by the public, including the narthex, nave, transepts, chancel, chapels, choir loft, side altars and main altar. Areas not open to and not ordinarily seen by the public, including the sacristies, vesting rooms, basements, upper floors or attic areas, organ chambers, closets, service areas, and the entire interior of the parsonage are not hereby subject to consideration. Areas made subject to Historic District Commission consideration are shown on the floor plan on file in the Offices of the City Clerk, the Historic Designation Advisory Board, and the Historic District Commission.

(2) In considering proposals for the alteration, demolition, partial demolition, removal, or addi-

DETROIT CITY CODE

tion to any or all of the architectural features and permanent furnishings within the designated areas of the interior of Zion Lutheran Church, the Historic District Commission shall use the following criteria:

a. Subsections (d)(1) through (22) of this section, as applicable;

b. The architectural or historic significance of the existing or proposed structure, feature, permanent furnishing fixture, and its relationship to the architectural and historic value of the Zion Lutheran Church Historic District;

c. The purpose of the designated spaces within the Zion Lutheran Church and the needs of its owners, provided, that such considerations shall not bind the Historic District Commission to permit any work solely on the basis of such considerations;

laws.title: Ste. Anne’s Parish Complex Historic District
laws.content:
(a) An historic district to be known as the Ste. Anne’s Parish Complex Historic District is hereby established in accordance with the provisions of this article.

(b) This historic district designation is hereby certified as being consistent with the Detroit Master Plan of Policies.

(c) The boundaries of the Ste. Anne’s Parish Complex Historic District, as shown on the map on file in the Office of the City Clerk, are as follows:

On the south the center line of West Lafayette Boulevard; on the west the center line of Ste. Anne Street; on the north the center line of Howard Street (now closed); and on the east the center line of the north-south alley lying between Ste. Anne Street and 18th Street. The legal description is lots 1 through 17 of Canfield’s Subdivision of the Loranger Farm, which is found at Liber 7, Page 82, of the County of Wayne Tract Index.

(d) The elements of design, as defined in Section 21-2-2 of this Code, shall be as follows:

(1) Height. The buildings of the Ste. Anne’s Parish Complex vary in the number of stories and height. The church is a tall single-story space that is approximately 40 feet in height to the eaves according to the Sanborn Maps, which list the height of the towers at the northern corners of the church as being 180 feet. The rectory is $2\frac{1}{2}$ stories tall, meaning that it has two full stories and an attic space. The school is $3\frac{1}{2}$ stories tall, meaning that it has three full stories and an attic space. The convent is $2\frac{1}{2}$ stories tall meaning that it has two full stories and an attic space. The hall is $1\frac{1}{2}$ stories tall, with walls one story in height and a tall roof into which the interior space projects.

(2) Proportion of buildings’ front façades. The façade of the church is taller than wide due to the towers, but gives an impression of balance with its tall towers widely spaced on either side of the central façade. The side elevations of the church are wider than tall to their eaves, and there is no visible rear elevation because of the abutting chapel. The rectory appears originally to have been proportioned vertically, but the later addition of the extensive porch on the west and south sides balance the façades by introducing a strong horizontal element. The convent façade is balanced. The school façade is balanced, but the central gable and the cupola tend to create a feeling of verticality. The hall is rather horizontal in feeling because of the wider base and the narrower two-story central bay.

(3) Proportion of openings within the façades. Openings in the façade of the church amount to approximately five percent. All openings are taller than wide except for the circular window centered in the central bay. Openings on other façades of the church are similarly proportioned. Openings in other buildings occupy a higher percentage of wall area, varying from building to building. In general, openings are taller than wide. In some instances, individual openings, which are taller than wide, are combined in a single opening and divided by a mullion or mullions; in such cases the total opening may be balanced or wider than tall. The horizontal windows over the infill in the openings on the south side of the rectory porch were added later and are uncharacteristic.

(4) Rhythm of solids to voids in front façades. The front façade of the church is divided into three sections: the center main gabled section and the two projecting tower sections at the outer ends. The gaps between the central gable wall and the towers are an important design element of this building. The large stained glass circular window in the façade is positioned above the central entrance opening. There are ogival windows arranged symmetrically in the façade, and blind arcading is a feature that occurs in several locations. The octagonal upper stages of the towers

CD21:185
§ 21-2-165

DETROIT CITY CODE

have one tall ogival opening filled with lowers on each face. The side elevation of the church on Ste. Anne Street has its openings regularly arranged. Although not fully symmetrical, the openings in the front façade of the rectory are also regularly arranged. The Mansard roof has dormers arranged above the windows in the wall below. The openings in the front façades of the school, convent, and hall are fully symmetrical and regularly arranged.

(5) *Rhythm of spacing of buildings on streets.* Not applicable due to single-complex district.

(6) *Rhythm of entrance and/or porch projections.* Because of the relationship of the separate buildings that make up the complex, no rhythm is established.

(7) *Relationship of materials.* Detroit common brick is the dominant material of the complex. Stone is commonly used for decorative purposes, for sills, and for other functional elements. The whole lower level of the church façade is stone. The church and hall retain slate roofs, while the other buildings have been reroofed in asphalt shingle. Wood trim is commonplace. The church façade and towers have sheet metal elements originally meant to imitate stone.

(8) *Relationship of textures.* The major textural relationship is that of common brick laid in mortar. The slate roofs contribute significantly to textural interest, while the asphalt roofs do not. Wood, which is generally smooth, is commonly used for the trim and functional elements such as windows and doors. Secondary textural relationships exist, such as the juxtaposition of stone trim with common brick, the rock-faced texture of the stone base of the church façade, and the use of sheet metal elements. The glazing on all buildings, especially the church, provides a contrasting smooth surface.

(9) *Relationship of color.* The orange-red of Detroit common brick is the predominant color, and in some cases is darkened with age and dirt. The roofs of the church and hall are composed of natural color slate, with gray being the most predominant color. Stone colors contrast with the common brick. The copper trim has weathered to a shade of green. Wood trim is usually painted brown, although other colors might be appropriate. In some places, the sheet metal is painted stone color, in imitation of stone, and is appropriate. The natural wood doors of the church contrast with the stone color of the base of the façade.

(10) *Relationship of architectural details.*

a. The architectural elements and details of Ste. Anne’s Church reflect its Gothic Revival Style. Buttresses exist to the sides of the entrances, at the corners of the front façade, at the transition between the main bay of the front façade and the bays dividing them from the towers, on the side elevations at the corners, and between aisle windows. The two towers, with their steeples, have had some details removed since their construction, but still display typical details such as pinnacles. Above the molded and carved central doorway in the gable of the main section of the church façade is a blind arcade and a large traceried circular window. Within the apex of the large gable is a blind triple arch. There is a small cupola in "fleche" position on the roof at the intersection of the nave and transepts.

b. Details of the other buildings conform to their styles and types. The school is vaguely Gothic or Tudor Revival with buttresses which flank the entrance and at the corners of the façade, and with a cupola with ogival openings. The rectory’s appearance has been greatly altered by the addition of large porches with masonry piers to the west and south. The house was originally an eclectic design with a Mansard roof. The details of the rectory itself are in accord with the usual treatment of eclectic Victorian residences of the 1880s, while the porches have a strong Prairie and/or Arts and Crafts character. The convent is Romanesque Revival in style with strong architectural elements, such as arched windows and relatively simple surfaces which are typical of that style. The hall is designed in a Classical manner with quoins laid in the brick, a triple-arched arcade in the second floor of the façade, and a classical pediment. Its details are in accordance with the Classical manner.

(11) *Relationship of roof shapes.* The main roof of the church is a front-facing gable with a trans-

CD21:186

laws.title: History
laws.content:
§ 21-2-165

verse gable over the crossing and transepts. The towers are roofed with tall steeples. The rectory has a Mansard roof interrupted by dormers. The convent has a side-facing gabled roof flanked by gabled parapet walls and fronted by a pair of wall dormers. A small dormer lies higher in the roof between the wall dormers. The hall has a broad hip roof, the upper central portion of which is carried forward as a front-facing gable roof. The school has intersecting hipped roofs with a tall wall dormer centered on the front and a cupola at the intersection of the ridges.

(12) *Walls of continuity.* Because of the small size of the district, the walls of continuity tend to be weakened; however, the church and school share a similar setback on the Howard Street frontage. The church, chapel, garage, and rectory form a strong wall of continuity on St. Anne Street. The side of the rectory, the hall, and the convent form a strong wall of continuity on West Lafayette Boulevard.

(13) *Relationship of significant landscape features and surface treatments.* The church faces a public space created by the closure of Howard Street. The surface treatments and plantings are typical of the 1970s. The Ste. Anne frontage is characterized by a grass turf lawn and modest plantings lying between the public sidewalk and the church, chapel, and rectory, with a drive leading to the garage. The setback on West Lafayette Boulevard is very shallow, but is consistent, and there are areas of grass turf lawn and plantings. There is a recent timber-built wheelchair ramp in front of the convent. An asphalt parking lot occupies the space that is between the church and school, and behind the school, convent, and hall. There is a State of Michigan Historical Marker on the lawn at the northwest corner of the property.

(14) *Relationship of open space to structures.* The public space in front of the church is intended to serve as a forecourt to a landmark building. The open space on the Ste. Anne frontage consists of the setback to the building line and modest plantings. There is a little open space on West Lafayette Boulevard since the setback is shallow. The parking area in the center of the property and between the church and school tends to be invisible except when viewed from the Howard Street side and from within the space itself.

There are dwellings located across from the property on Ste. Anne Street and considerable vacant land in both residential and commercial areas around the property that is partially due to decline and partially due to clearance.

(15) *Scale of façades and façade elements.* The Ste. Anne’s Parish Complex rises above the residential and commercial structures that surround it. In that context, its scale is grand, although only the church is of monumental scale. Major elements of the church such as towers, spires, transepts, and apses, are also large in scale. Other buildings are less monumental, but still contain the large elements typical of buildings of a public character.

(16) *Directional expression of front elevations.* In general, the original directional expression of all the buildings, except the hall and school, was vertical. In the church, the wide spread of the towers reduces the vertical impression, but the façade is distinctly taller than wide. The added porches of the rectory are opposed to its original vertical expression, and the building now tends to balance. The convent retains its vertical expression. The hall has always tended to a horizontal expression of the front elevation. The school tends to the vertical, although the original two-story building, prior to the addition of the third floor, was likely horizontal in expression.

(17) *Rhythm of building setbacks.* Little rhythm is established in this district with few buildings.

(18) *Relationship of lot coverage.* There is no standard range of lot coverage among separate properties because this is a single complex and the buildings vary greatly in size. The buildings of the complex as a whole occupy between 40 percent and 45 percent of the property.

(19) *Degree of complexity within the façades.* The façade of the church, rectory, convent, school, and hall are all fairly straightforward in their arrangements of elements, but display some complexity of details. Overall, there is a fair degree of complexity.

(20) *Orientation, vistas, overviews.* The church and school are oriented toward Howard Street, now a vacated public space. The side of the church, chapel, garage, and rectory orient to Ste. Anne Street and form a strong, but not straight, con-

CD21:187
§ 21-2-165

DETROIT CITY CODE

tinuous wall of buildings. The hall and convent orient to West Lafayette Boulevard, with the side wall of the rectory forming an additional element of that street face. Ste. Anne’s Church serves as an impressive landmark as viewed from the Fisher Freeway and the Ambassador Bridge when entering the United States from Canada.

(21) Symmetric or asymmetric appearance. The front of the church is symmetrical in appearance. The front façades of the hall, school, and convent are symmetrical. The rectory is asymmetrical, but was originally a balanced composition.

(22) General environmental character. The complex is located in a mixed-use area, with a declining residential area to the east, west and north; commercial uses often associated with the Ambassador Bridge are nearby to the west and to the south. New development is proposed for the area both for residential and commercial purposes. This is, and will likely remain, a mixed-use urban area. The Ste. Anne’s Parish Complex is a physical reminder of this religious institution’s role as a focal point of the community.

(e) In accordance with Section 21-2-76 of this Code, the Historic District Commission is hereby authorized to consider interior features in certain portions of Ste. Anne’s Church, which is located within the Ste. Anne’s Parish Complex Historic District. A permit shall be required for such interior work in those portions of Ste. Anne’s Church, as required in Section 21-2-71 of this Code, as if such work were exterior work. The Historic District Commission’s consideration of the interior features of the Ste. Anne’s Church, as provided for in Section 21-2-76 of this Code, shall be as follows:

(1) The interior spaces of Ste. Anne’s Church which are hereby made subject to the Historic District Commission’s consideration are those spaces normally open to or seen by the public, including the narthex (or vestibule), nave, side aisles, transepts, chancel, bases of towers, chapel, choir loft, side altar, and main altar apses or chapels. Areas not open to and not ordinarily seen by the public, including the sacristies, vesting rooms, basements, upper floors or attic areas, organ chambers, closets, service areas and the entire interiors of the rectory, school, hall, garage, and convent are not subject to the Historic District Commission’s review and consideration.

(2) When considering proposals for the alteration, demolition, partial demolition, removal, or addition to any or all of the architectural features and permanent furnishings within the designated areas of the interior of Ste. Anne’s Church, the Historic District Commission shall use the following criteria:

a. Subsections (d)(1) through (22) of this section, as applicable;

b. The architectural or historic significance of the existing or proposed structure, feature, permanent furnishing or fixture, and its relationship to the architectural and historical value of the Ste. Anne’s Parish Complex Historic District;

c. The purpose of the designated spaces within the Ste. Anne’s Parish Complex and the needs of its owners, provided, that such considerations shall not bind the Historic District Commission to permit any work solely on the basis of such considerations;

d. The provisions of Section 21-2-75 of this Code; and

e. Any other factor, including aesthetics, which the Historic District Commission deems to be pertinent.

(3) As a guide in considering proposals affecting the designated interior spaces of the Ste. Anne’s Parish Complex, the Historic District Commission shall make use of a set of slides, taken by the staff of the Historic Designation Advisory Board prior to the effective date of this section, which was December 16, 1997, and represents the state of those interior spaces as of the date of designation. A copy of this set of slides, together with a list describing each slide and a diagram showing the relationship of the slides to the designated interior spaces, shall be placed on file in the Offices of the City Clerk, the Historic Designation Advisory Board, the Historic District Commission, and the Burton Historical Collection of the Detroit Public Library. (Code 1984, § 25-2-127; Ord. No. 42-97, § 1(25-2-127), eff. 12-16-1997)

laws.title: Moses W. Field House Historic District
laws.content:
(a) An historic district to be known as the Moses W. Field House Historic District is hereby established in accordance with the provisions of this article.

(b) This historic district designation is hereby certified as being consistent with the Detroit Master Plan of Policies.

(c) The boundaries of the Moses W. Field House Historic District, as shown on the map on file in the Office of the City Clerk, are as follows:

On the north, the north line of Lot 61 of Frontenac Subdivision (Liber 24, Page 31), extended east and west; on the east, the center line of Field Avenue; on the south, the south line of Lot 62 of Frontenac Subdivision (Liber 24, Page 31), extended east and west; and on the west, the center line of the north-south alley between Field Avenue and East Grand Boulevard.

(d) The elements of design, as defined in Section 21-2-2 of this Code, shall be as follows:

(1) *Height.* The Moses W. Field House, the primary building of the Moses W. Field House Historic District, is two stories tall on a high basement with a 1½-story addition in the rear. The detached garage is one story tall with a tall hip roof.

(2) *Proportion of building’s front façades.* The front façade of the Moses W. Field House is approximately as tall to its eaves as it is wide.

(3) *Proportion of openings within the façades.* Openings amount to approximately 25 percent of the façade of the Moses W. Field House. All of the openings are taller than wide except for the basement windows, which are wider than tall.

(4) *Rhythm of solids to voids in front façades.* The front façade of the Moses W. Field House is divided into three vertical bays, with one opening per bay in each of the two stories. Openings of first- and second-story windows and the front single-door entrance are segmentally arched. The windows are double-hung, each sash subdivided into two lights divided by a single vertical muntin. The first floor windows, or front parlor windows, extend up from the floor level; each side wall of the primary shallow first floor entrance projection is punctured by a single, slender double-hung sash window. A rectangular

CD21:191
§ 21-2-167

DETROIT CITY CODE

bay containing a pair of subdivided double-hung sash windows extends out from the south elevation; a similar paired arrangement of windows is positioned in the flat wall surface above at second-story level. The other window openings in the side elevations are regularly spaced and segmentally arched, containing similarly subdivided double-hung sashes.

(5) *Rhythm of spacing of buildings on streets.* The Moses W. Field House Historic District is composed of one primary building that is set back noticeably further on its lot than the primary buildings on the adjoining lots.

(6) *Rhythm of entrance and/or porch projections.* The first-floor entrance bay projects slightly from the body of the house, and the porch extends further out in front of the entrance, with six steps leading up to it from the ground level. Originally, the porch extended almost the entire width of the first floor. A wooden porch has been added to the back of the rear addition, and a hatch to the cellar projects from the rear (west) elevation of the original house.

(7) *Relationship of materials.* Detroit common brick is the dominant material of the Moses W. Field House. The rear addition is sheathed in clapboard. The original building rests on brick foundations that were covered with stucco circa 1905. The addition rests on concrete block. Window and doors sills are masonry, as are the steps and stair walls. Wood elements occur in the form of porch pilasters, shutters, window frames, fascia boards, soffits and brackets. An iron railing lines the sides of the front porch. The garage is wood with an asphalt shingle roof.

(8) *Relationship of textures.* The major texture is that of common brick laid in mortar. The stuccoed foundations have incised lines that resemble mortar joints, creating the appearance of stone blocks. The rear clapboard addition contrasts with the brick body of the original house. Wood is commonly used for trim and functional elements and is generally smooth. Secondary textural relationships exist, such as the juxtaposition of scored and unscored masonry sills with common brick. The garage is sided with clapboard. The asphalt shingle roofs of the house and garage do not generally contribute to textural interest.

(9) *Relationship of colors.* The natural orange-red of Detroit common brick emerging through scaling light gray paint is the dominant color. Limestone-colored paint, where it is used on the foundations and sills, contrasts with the common brick; the window sills on the front façade are red sandstone under the paint. The rear clapboard addition is painted bluegray. Wood elements are usually painted blue with brackets under the eaves of the main roof presently primed white. The garage is painted bluish gray.

(10) *Relationship of architectural details.* The architectural elements and details generally relate to the Victorian Italianate style, such as the low-pitched hip roof with widely overhanging eaves supported by large brackets, the bracketed porch and side bay roofs, the elongated double-hung windows, and the visually-balanced façade.

(11) *Relationship of roof shapes.* The main roof of the Moses W. Field House is a shallow hip. The porch roof and the roof over the side bay are flat. The garage at the rear of the lot has a steep hip roof.

(12) *Walls of continuity.* Not applicable due to single-building district.

(13) *Relationship of significant landscape features and surface treatments.* A wide, graded tree lawn planted with an old maple tree is located between the curb and the public sidewalk in front of the Moses W. Field House property. This tree lawn contains a set of concrete steps leading from the curb to the public sidewalk. A row of hedges close to the public sidewalk somewhat hides the house from public view. A grass turf front yard is divided by a straight concrete walk on axis leading up to the house. Two crab apple trees, one on either side of the walk, are located close to the front porch; a catalpa tree is located in the northeast corner of the front yard. On the unimproved grass turf side lot in the front is an old and significant apple tree, and in the back yard is an old and significant pear tree. Much of the yard in the rear of the house is paved in brick, with a concrete sidewalk along the north side of the house extending from front to back. To the south of the house, the unimproved lot is of grass turf. A chain-link fence extending out from the rear corners of the house is located around the perimeter of the rear of the property.
